q: A private firm logs into a government portal to file its GST returns. Which e-governance interaction model does this represent?

opts.A: G2C
opts.B: G2B
opts.C: G2G
opts.D: G2E

exp: The counterparty decides the model, and here the government is dealing with a business, so it is G2B (Government to Business), which covers licences, tenders, procurement and tax filing. G2C would apply if an individual citizen were paying his own income tax; the type of tax does not decide the model.

q: A district office scans its old paper land records and stores them as PDF files, while the approval workflow continues exactly as before. This activity is best described as

opts.A: digitalisation
opts.B: digital transformation
opts.C: digitisation
opts.D: business process re-engineering

exp: Digitisation is simply converting analog content into digital form, which is exactly what scanning records into PDF does. Digitalisation would mean using the digital record to change how the process runs, and digital transformation goes further still by reorganising what the office does around the citizen.

sub: Emerging Technologies: Artificial Intelligence (AI), Internet of Things (IoT), Blockchain, Big Data, Cloud Computing and Edge Computing
q: A factory safety system must shut down a machine within milliseconds of a sensor reading, and the plant has a slow internet link. Which approach best suits this requirement?

opts.A: Edge computing, processing the sensor data on or beside the machine
opts.B: Cloud computing, sending every reading to a remote data centre for analysis
opts.C: Blockchain, recording every sensor reading in a distributed ledger
opts.D: Big data analytics, storing the readings for later batch processing

exp: Edge computing processes data at or near its source, which cuts both latency and bandwidth use and is why latency-critical work such as a safety cut-off belongs at the edge. Cloud computing centralises processing in distant data centres, so the network round trip alone would exceed the millisecond budget.

sub: Emerging Technologies: Artificial Intelligence (AI), Internet of Things (IoT), Blockchain, Big Data, Cloud Computing and Edge Computing
q: Volume, Velocity and Variety are the three core characteristics used to define

opts.A: edge computing
opts.B: blockchain
opts.C: the Internet of Things
opts.D: big data

exp: Big data is characterised by the three Vs of Volume, Velocity and Variety, with Veracity and Value commonly added; it is defined by these properties and not by any threshold in gigabytes. IoT is a major source that feeds big data, but it is not itself defined by the Vs.

q: A government server room runs twelve lightly loaded physical servers. Which green computing measure would give the largest practical energy saving?

opts.A: Replacing the CRT monitors on the admin consoles with LED monitors
opts.B: Virtualisation and server consolidation onto a few well-utilised hosts
opts.C: Enabling display timeout on the administrator workstations
opts.D: Switching to double-sided printing for server documentation

exp: Virtualisation and server consolidation raise the utilisation of a small number of physical machines and retire the rest, which is the largest practical energy saving available in a server room. The other measures are genuine green practices but affect peripherals and paper, not the racks that consume most of the power.

q: Which statement correctly describes the purpose of these environmental marks and standards?

opts.A: ENERGY STAR restricts hazardous substances, while RoHS rates energy efficiency
opts.B: Both ENERGY STAR and RoHS rate the energy efficiency of equipment
opts.C: ENERGY STAR and EPEAT rate energy efficiency and environmental performance, while RoHS restricts hazardous substances
opts.D: EPEAT restricts hazardous substances, while ENERGY STAR governs e-waste collection

exp: ENERGY STAR and EPEAT are ratings for energy efficiency and environmental performance of equipment, whereas RoHS is a restriction on hazardous substances such as lead, mercury and cadmium in electrical and electronic goods. The two purposes are routinely swapped in options, so read which one rates and which one restricts.

q: In the traditional two-chip motherboard chipset design, which group of interfaces was handled by the southbridge?

opts.A: The connection between the CPU and main memory
opts.B: The AGP or PCI Express graphics interface
opts.C: The CPU's internal cache and register file
opts.D: USB, SATA, audio and LAN

exp: The southbridge handled the slower peripheral I/O such as USB, SATA, audio, LAN and legacy buses, while the northbridge sat on the high-speed side handling CPU-to-memory and CPU-to-graphics traffic. Any option attaching a USB port or keyboard to the northbridge is wrong.

q: The chipset of a motherboard mainly determines

opts.A: which CPU families, memory types and expansion interfaces the board can support
opts.B: the clock speed at which the processor executes instructions
opts.C: the physical dimensions and mounting-hole pattern of the board
opts.D: the amount of cache memory available inside the processor

exp: The chipset is the controller silicon between the CPU and the rest of the board, and it fixes which CPU families, memory speeds and expansion interfaces the board can take. Physical dimensions and mounting are decided by the form factor such as ATX or Mini-ITX, while clock speed and cache are properties of the processor itself.

q: A processor is described as 4C/8T. How will the operating system see it?

opts.A: As eight physical cores, each running one thread
opts.B: As four physical processors in four separate sockets
opts.C: As eight logical processors provided by four physical cores
opts.D: As four cores that can each run only one thread at a time

exp: In 4C/8T notation the 8 is the thread count, so four physical cores using simultaneous multi-threading present themselves to the operating system as eight logical processors. Logical processors are not physical cores; they fill execution slots a single thread leaves idle, so the gain is a useful fraction rather than a doubling.

q: An office replaces a dual-core PC with an octa-core PC, but the accounting application it runs is entirely single-threaded. What is the most likely outcome for that application?

opts.A: It will run about four times faster because there are four times as many cores
opts.B: Its speed will change little, since a single-threaded program can use only one core at a time
opts.C: It will run slower, because work must be divided among eight cores
opts.D: It will automatically be split across all eight cores by the processor

exp: Extra cores raise throughput only for software written to use them, so a single-threaded program still executes on one core and sees little benefit. Amdahl's Law makes the same point generally: the serial fraction of a program cannot be sped up by adding cores.

q: Which protocols does a NAS appliance typically use to serve data to its clients?

opts.A: NFS and SMB/CIFS
opts.B: iSCSI and Fibre Channel
opts.C: SMTP and IMAP
opts.D: SNMP and SSH

exp: A NAS is file-level storage and serves files using network file-sharing protocols: NFS on Unix and Linux, SMB/CIFS on Windows. iSCSI and Fibre Channel are block-level storage protocols and belong to a SAN, which presents raw disk rather than files.

q: A directorate wants a single place where several clerks can open and save the same documents over the existing office LAN, appearing on each PC as a mapped network drive. Which is the most appropriate solution?

opts.A: A Fibre Channel SAN with a LUN presented to each PC
opts.B: An external USB hard disk attached to the head clerk's PC
opts.C: An additional internal hard disk in each clerk's PC
opts.D: A NAS appliance on the office Ethernet network

exp: A NAS serves files over the ordinary Ethernet LAN and appears to each client as a shared folder or mapped drive, with the appliance handling locking so several clerks can use the same share at once. A SAN would present raw blocks that look like a local disk, and two machines writing to the same LUN would corrupt it without a cluster-aware file system.

q: When a LUN from a SAN is presented to a server, how does it appear to that server's operating system?

opts.A: As a shared folder that must be mounted with NFS or SMB
opts.B: As a web page served by the storage array's management interface
opts.C: As a local, unformatted disk that the server itself partitions and formats
opts.D: As a read-only archive that cannot hold a file system

exp: A SAN provides block-level access, so the array hands over raw blocks and the server partitions the LUN, creates the file system on it and mounts it, exactly as it would an internal drive. Appearing as a shared folder reached over NFS or SMB is the behaviour of a NAS, which serves files rather than blocks.

q: An office deploys iSCSI storage that runs over its ordinary Ethernet network using standard NICs. Is this a SAN or a NAS, and why?

opts.A: A NAS, because it uses ordinary Ethernet rather than a dedicated fabric
opts.B: A SAN, because access is at block level even though the cabling is Ethernet
opts.C: A NAS, because no Fibre Channel host bus adapters are involved
opts.D: Neither, because a SAN must always use Fibre Channel

exp: It is the access level, block versus file, that decides whether storage is a SAN or a NAS, not the type of cable, so iSCSI over ordinary Ethernet is still a SAN. iSCSI needs only a standard NIC and an iSCSI initiator instead of a Fibre Channel HBA, which is why it is the affordable route for small and mid-size sites.

q: A server is backed up fully every Sunday and differentially on every other day. To restore the server after a failure on Thursday, what is needed?

opts.A: The Sunday full backup plus only Wednesday's differential backup
opts.B: The Sunday full backup plus every differential backup from Monday to Wednesday in order
opts.C: Only Wednesday's differential backup
opts.D: Every full backup taken since the server was commissioned

exp: A differential backup copies everything changed since the last full backup, so a restore needs only the last full plus the most recent differential. Needing the full plus every intervening backup in sequence is the incremental scheme, where each job copies only what changed since the last backup of any kind.

q: The 3-2-1 rule of backup states that an organisation should keep

opts.A: three full backups, two incremental backups and one differential backup
opts.B: three backups a day, two verifications a week and one test restore a month
opts.C: three years of retention, two catalogues and one archive copy
opts.D: three copies of the data, on two different media, with one copy offsite

exp: The 3-2-1 rule means three copies of the data, held on two different media or systems, with at least one copy kept offsite so a single site disaster cannot destroy everything. Ransomware has added a further idea that one copy should be offline or immutable, but the rule itself is about copies, media and location, not about backup types or schedules.

q: A department decides that after any failure it can afford to lose at most fifteen minutes of transactions, and therefore replicates its database every fifteen minutes. Which disaster recovery objective is it setting?

opts.A: Recovery Time Objective (RTO)
opts.B: Recovery Point Objective (RPO)
opts.C: Mean Time Between Failures (MTBF)
opts.D: Service Level Agreement (SLA)

exp: RPO is the maximum tolerable data loss, looking backwards from the incident, and it is achieved by setting backup or replication frequency, which is exactly what a fifteen-minute replication interval does. RTO is the different question of how long the service may remain down, and is achieved by standby capacity and rehearsed procedure.

q: A DR plan specifies RPO = 1 hour and RTO = 4 hours. Which statement interprets this correctly?

opts.A: Up to 4 hours of data may be lost, and the service must be restored within 1 hour
opts.B: The service must be restored within 5 hours in total, with no data loss permitted
opts.C: Up to 1 hour of data may be lost, and the service must be restored within 4 hours
opts.D: Backups must be taken every 4 hours and tested every hour

exp: RPO is the data-loss tolerance and RTO is the downtime tolerance, so an RPO of one hour permits losing at most an hour's data while an RTO of four hours requires the service to be running again within four hours. Swapping the two is the standard error: RPO looks back at data, RTO looks forward at time.

q: A rugged handheld terminal must be operated by field staff wearing gloves. Which touchscreen technology is suitable?

opts.A: A capacitive touchscreen, because it senses a change in an electric field
opts.B: A capacitive touchscreen, because it supports multi-touch gestures
opts.C: An optical touchscreen, because gloves reflect infrared light
opts.D: A resistive touchscreen, because it registers physical pressure from any object

exp: A resistive screen works by pressure between two conductive layers, so it responds to a gloved hand or any stylus, which is why it survives on rugged field devices and older POS terminals. A capacitive screen needs a conductive touch such as a bare finger and will not respond to an ordinary glove, whatever its multi-touch advantages.

q: Which technology is used to read the answer sheets of a competitive examination, where candidates darken bubbles with a pencil?

opts.A: OMR
opts.B: OCR
opts.C: MICR
opts.D: RFID

exp: OMR, optical mark recognition, detects the presence of marks at fixed positions on a form, which is exactly how bubble answer sheets are read. OCR recognises the shapes of printed or written characters and MICR reads magnetic-ink characters on cheques, so the three are not interchangeable.

q: A genuine, enrolled employee repeatedly fails to be recognised by the office fingerprint attendance device. This is an instance of

opts.A: a false acceptance, measured by the FAR
opts.B: an equal error, measured by the EER
opts.C: a false rejection, measured by the FRR
opts.D: a failure to enrol, measured by the FTE

exp: FRR, the false rejection rate, is the proportion of genuine users wrongly refused, which is a usability failure of exactly this kind. FAR is the opposite error of admitting an impostor, and failure to enrol describes a person whose biometric could not be registered in the first place, not one already enrolled who is being turned away.

q: Why is the compromise of a person's stored fingerprint data considered more serious than the compromise of that person's password?

opts.A: Fingerprint data occupies far more storage space than a password
opts.B: A fingerprint is an identifier that cannot be changed or reissued, whereas a password can be replaced
opts.C: Fingerprint matching is performed without any encryption of the sample
opts.D: A fingerprint can be used only for identification and never for verification

exp: Biometrics are identifiers rather than secrets: you leave fingerprints on everything you touch, and a compromised fingerprint cannot be reissued the way a password can simply be reset. Encryption is in fact required in Indian practice, where Aadhaar authentication must use STQC-certified registered devices that encrypt the sample inside the sensor.

q: A paper letter has been scanned and saved as a PDF. What further step is needed before the text in that PDF can be searched and edited?

opts.A: Compressing the PDF so that its file size is reduced
opts.B: Running OCR (Optical Character Recognition) over the scanned image
opts.C: Rescanning the page at a higher dpi setting
opts.D: Converting the file to PDF/A for long-term archiving

exp: A scanner produces only a picture of the page, so the characters are dots, not text; OCR is the separate step that converts those images of characters into character codes that can be searched and edited. Raising the dpi produces a sharper image but still an image, and PDF/A conversion only fixes the preservation format.

q: In a scanner's specifications, which resolution figure represents the detail the sensor genuinely captures?

opts.A: Interpolated resolution
opts.B: Enhanced resolution
opts.C: Optical resolution
opts.D: Output resolution of the attached printer

exp: Optical resolution is what the CCD or CIS sensor array actually records, and it is the figure worth quoting. Interpolated or 'enhanced' resolution is software enlargement of the captured image and adds no real detail, which is why it is treated as a marketing number.

q: Which statement correctly distinguishes a resistive touchscreen from an ordinary capacitive touchscreen?

opts.A: A resistive screen responds to pressure from any object, while a capacitive screen needs a conductive touch such as a bare finger
opts.B: A capacitive screen responds to any object, while a resistive screen works only with a bare finger
opts.C: Both need a conductive object, but only the resistive type can register a touch at all
opts.D: A resistive screen gives better clarity and native multi-touch than a capacitive screen

exp: A resistive screen has two conductive layers pressed together at the point of contact, so a gloved finger or a plastic stylus works; a capacitive screen senses a change in an electrostatic field and therefore needs a conductive touch. The trade-off runs the other way on quality: capacitive screens give the better clarity and easy multi-touch.

q: What is the correct difference between an interactive whiteboard and an interactive flat panel display?

opts.A: They are two names for the same device
opts.B: An interactive whiteboard cannot accept touch input; it is an output device only
opts.C: An interactive flat panel needs an external projector, while a whiteboard has its own screen
opts.D: An interactive whiteboard needs an external projector, while an interactive flat panel is a self-contained display

exp: An interactive whiteboard is a projection surface, so it depends on a separate projector and computer and washes out in a bright room. An interactive flat panel display carries the screen, touch layer and speakers in one unit, which is why it has become the default choice for smart classrooms.

q: In the term 'free software', what does the word 'free' refer to?

opts.A: That the program can always be downloaded at no cost
opts.B: That the program carries no copyright at all
opts.C: The user's freedom to run, study, modify and redistribute the program
opts.D: That the program may be used without payment for a trial period

exp: Free software is defined by the four freedoms - to run the program for any purpose, to study and change it, to redistribute copies, and to distribute modified versions - which is why access to the source code is essential. Free here means freedom, not price: copies of GPL-licensed software may lawfully be sold.

q: Software that is distributed at no cost, but without its source code and without any right to modify it, is called

opts.A: freeware
opts.B: open source software
opts.C: public domain software
opts.D: free software

exp: Freeware is proprietary software given away at zero price - vendor document readers and drivers are the usual examples - and the user receives only the binary. Open source and free software both require the source code and the right to modify, while public domain software carries no copyright and so imposes no conditions at all.

q: What is the essential difference between a virtual machine and a container?

opts.A: A container runs its own complete guest operating system, while a virtual machine does not
opts.B: A virtual machine starts in a few seconds, while a container boots like a physical computer
opts.C: A container provides stronger isolation than a virtual machine
opts.D: A virtual machine runs a full guest operating system, while a container shares the host operating system's kernel

exp: A virtual machine carries an entire guest operating system on top of a hypervisor, so it is sized in gigabytes and boots like a physical machine; a container packages only the application and its dependencies and calls the shared host kernel, so it is sized in megabytes and starts in seconds. That sharing also means a container's isolation is weaker, not stronger, than a virtual machine's.

q: VMware ESXi and Microsoft Hyper-V are examples of

opts.A: Type 2 (hosted) hypervisors
opts.B: Type 1 (bare-metal) hypervisors
opts.C: container runtimes
opts.D: container orchestration platforms

exp: A Type 1 or bare-metal hypervisor runs directly on the hardware with no host operating system beneath it, which is what data centres deploy; ESXi, Hyper-V, Xen and KVM are of this kind. VirtualBox and VMware Workstation are Type 2, running as applications on a desktop operating system, while Docker is a container runtime and Kubernetes an orchestrator.

q: Which statement about Java and JavaScript is correct?

opts.A: They are unrelated languages that merely share part of their name
opts.B: JavaScript is a lightweight version of Java meant for use inside the browser
opts.C: JavaScript programs are compiled to Java bytecode and executed on the JVM
opts.D: Java is the browser's client-side scripting language and JavaScript is its server-side counterpart

exp: The shared name is a marketing accident: Java is statically typed and compiled to bytecode for the JVM, while JavaScript is dynamically typed, standardised as ECMAScript, and runs in browser engines and on servers through Node.js. Neither language is a version or subset of the other.

q: Why must data validation done by JavaScript in the browser always be repeated on the server?

opts.A: Because JavaScript is unable to check numeric values
opts.B: Because the server executes the same script much faster
opts.C: Because client-side script is visible to the user and can be altered or bypassed
opts.D: Because browsers keep JavaScript disabled by default

exp: Client-side script is delivered to the user's machine and can be read through view-source or developer tools and switched off or edited, so it is only a convenience that gives quick feedback. Server-side code is never sent to the browser, so the server is the only place a validation rule can actually be enforced.

q: In a REST API, which HTTP method is normally used to read an existing resource?

opts.A: POST
opts.B: GET
opts.C: DELETE
opts.D: PUT

exp: REST maps operations onto standard HTTP methods: GET reads a resource, POST creates one, PUT or PATCH updates one, and DELETE removes one. POST is the common wrong pick because forms on web pages usually submit with it, but submitting a form is creating or sending data, not reading.

q: A REST API is described as 'stateless'. What does that mean?

opts.A: The API is forbidden from storing any data in a database
opts.B: The API returns an identical response to every request it receives
opts.C: The client must hold a permanent connection open to the server
opts.D: The server keeps no session information between calls, so each request carries everything needed to serve it

exp: Statelessness is about the conversation, not about storage: the server remembers nothing between one call and the next, so every request must include its own identification and parameters. The application behind the API may still read and write a database quite normally.

q: Under the Digital India programme, a document fetched into DigiLocker directly from its issuing authority

opts.A: is accepted for online applications only and never for physical verification
opts.B: must still be self-attested or attested by a gazetted officer
opts.C: is legally at par with the original physical document
opts.D: is treated only as a scanned copy with no legal standing

exp: A document pulled from the issuer into DigiLocker is issued electronically by that authority, so it carries the same legal standing as the original physical document and needs no further attestation. That is the distinction from a document a citizen has merely scanned and uploaded himself.

q: MeghRaj is the name of

opts.A: the Government of India's cloud computing initiative, the GI Cloud
opts.B: the network carrying broadband to gram panchayats
opts.C: the mobile app that aggregates central and state government services
opts.D: the government's online public procurement marketplace

exp: MeghRaj is the GI Cloud initiative, under which departmental applications are hosted on government cloud infrastructure. The other options describe BharatNet, UMANG and GeM respectively.

q: Which Indian law gives legal recognition to electronic records and to digital signatures, so that an electronic file is admissible in the same way as a paper one?

opts.A: The Public Records Act, 1993
opts.B: The Right to Information Act, 2005
opts.C: The Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023
opts.D: The Information Technology Act, 2000

exp: The Information Technology Act, 2000 is the statute that confers legal recognition on electronic records and on electronic and digital signatures. The Public Records Act, 1993 is a genuine records law but governs the management, retention and disposal of central government public records rather than the legal validity of electronic form.

q: In electronic records management, what is the difference between taking a backup and archiving a record?

opts.A: They are the same operation described by two different names
opts.B: A backup is a short-term copy kept for recovery, while archiving moves a record into preservation with metadata and a retention rule
opts.C: A backup is kept permanently, while an archive is deleted after a fixed period
opts.D: A backup carries metadata and retention rules, while an archive stores only the raw file

exp: A backup exists so that a system can be restored after failure and is overwritten on a cycle; archiving is a records action that places the record under a classification, metadata set and retention schedule so it stays authentic and retrievable for as long as required. Treating backups as an archive is the classic mistake, because a backup carries no retention rule and no index.

sub: Data Privacy and Personal Data Protection
q: Under the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023, the individual to whom the personal data relates is called the

opts.A: data principal
opts.B: data fiduciary
opts.C: data processor
opts.D: data protection officer

exp: The data principal is the human being the data is about; a parent or lawful guardian acts as principal for a child. The data fiduciary is the organisation that determines the purpose and means of processing and holds the data in trust, and a data processor only acts on that fiduciary's instructions.

sub: Data Privacy and Personal Data Protection
q: A department collects citizens' mobile numbers in order to send examination admit cards, and later uses the same numbers for an unrelated publicity campaign. Which data protection principle has been breached?

opts.A: Data minimisation
opts.B: Storage limitation
opts.C: Purpose limitation
opts.D: Reasonable security safeguards

exp: Purpose limitation requires personal data to be used only for the purpose for which it was notified and consented to, so reusing the numbers for a different purpose breaches it even though nothing was leaked. Data minimisation concerns collecting more fields than the purpose needs, and storage limitation concerns keeping data after the purpose is served.

q: An AI system used to shortlist applicants is found to consistently disadvantage one group. Where does such algorithmic bias most commonly originate?

opts.A: A coding error in the way the algorithm was implemented
opts.B: Skewed or unrepresentative data used to train the model
opts.C: Insufficient processing power on the server running the model
opts.D: The absence of encryption on the model's output

exp: A model learns the patterns present in its training data, so past unfairness or under-representation is reproduced and then applied at scale; the algorithm can be implemented perfectly and still discriminate. This is why removing names from the data does not cure bias - correlated features carry the same pattern.

q: In AI ethics, the expression 'human-in-the-loop' means that

opts.A: the system is trained only on data typed in manually by human operators
opts.B: responsibility for the outcome passes to the vendor who supplied the system
opts.C: humans may query the system but are not shown its output
opts.D: the AI produces a recommendation and a human being takes the final decision

exp: Human-in-the-loop keeps a person as the decision-maker with the AI acting only as an aid, and it is the expected safeguard wherever rights, money, liberty or entitlement are at stake. Accountability stays with the deploying officer and department; it does not shift to the model or the vendor.

q: The Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG) are built on four principles. They are

opts.A: Availability, Affordability, Skills and Language
opts.B: Authenticity, Integrity, Reliability and Usability
opts.C: Perceivable, Operable, Understandable and Robust
opts.D: Confidentiality, Integrity, Availability and Accountability

exp: WCAG, issued by the W3C, organises its requirements under Perceivable, Operable, Understandable and Robust, with conformance levels A, AA and AAA, of which AA is the usual target. The other sets belong elsewhere: the four axes of the digital divide, the qualities an electronic record must retain, and information-security principles.

q: Which Indian law makes it an obligation for government information, services and websites to be accessible to persons with disabilities?

opts.A: The Rights of Persons with Disabilities Act, 2016
opts.B: The Information Technology Act, 2000
opts.C: The Right to Information Act, 2005
opts.D: The Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023

exp: The Rights of Persons with Disabilities Act, 2016 requires government information and services, websites included, to be made accessible, so accessibility is a statutory duty rather than good practice. GIGW, the Guidelines for Indian Government Websites, is the compliance standard through which departments meet it.

q: On a Windows computer, what is the main difference between a Standard user account and an Administrator account?

opts.A: A Standard account cannot run applications that are already installed on the computer
opts.B: A Standard account may install software but may not change its own desktop settings
opts.C: A Standard account can run programs and change its own settings, but cannot install software or make system-wide changes without administrator approval
opts.D: A Standard account has full control of the computer but no access to the network

exp: The account type controls privilege, not capability: a Standard user works normally with applications and personal settings, but any change affecting the whole system requires an administrator's consent or credentials. Standard users can certainly run installed programs and reach the network, so the restriction is on system-wide change alone.

q: Why is it recommended that day-to-day work on a Windows machine be done from a Standard account rather than from an Administrator account?

opts.A: Malware or a mistaken action running under a Standard account cannot make system-wide changes without an explicit administrator approval
opts.B: Standard accounts make the computer start up faster
opts.C: Files created by a Standard account are automatically encrypted
opts.D: Standard accounts receive software updates before administrator accounts do

exp: This is the principle of least privilege: anything you run inherits your privileges, so working as a Standard user limits the damage a malicious or accidental action can do. Account type has no bearing on boot speed, encryption or update order.

q: What is the purpose of User Account Control (UAC) in Windows?

opts.A: It encrypts the contents of the hard disk so a stolen drive cannot be read
opts.B: It prompts for consent or for administrator credentials before an action that would change system settings is allowed to proceed
opts.C: It scans incoming email attachments for viruses
opts.D: It blocks unauthorised devices from connecting to the network

exp: UAC keeps even administrators running with reduced privilege and raises the familiar consent prompt whenever a program asks to elevate, so system-level changes cannot happen silently. Disk encryption is BitLocker's job and malware scanning is Microsoft Defender Antivirus's; UAC does neither.

q: Which built-in Windows feature encrypts an entire drive so that its data cannot be read if the disk is removed and attached to another computer?

opts.A: Windows Defender Firewall
opts.B: Microsoft Defender Antivirus
opts.C: User Account Control
opts.D: BitLocker Drive Encryption

exp: BitLocker performs full-volume encryption, so the contents remain unreadable without the correct credentials or recovery key even when the physical disk is moved to another machine. The firewall filters network traffic and the antivirus detects malicious files; neither protects a drive that has been physically taken.

q: What is Windows Terminal?

opts.A: A terminal application that can host several command-line shells, such as Command Prompt and PowerShell, in tabs within a single window
opts.B: A replacement for File Explorer that browses files graphically
opts.C: A remote desktop client used to connect to other Windows computers
opts.D: A new scripting language that replaces PowerShell

exp: Windows Terminal is a host, not a shell: it provides the window, tabs, panes and appearance settings, while the actual command interpreter running inside a tab may be Command Prompt, PowerShell or a Linux shell under WSL. It neither replaces Explorer nor introduces a language of its own.

q: Within Windows Terminal, which statement best describes PowerShell compared with the older Command Prompt (cmd.exe)?

opts.A: PowerShell runs only graphical applications, while Command Prompt runs only text ones
opts.B: PowerShell is a file manager, while Command Prompt is a shell
opts.C: PowerShell is a modern shell and scripting environment that passes structured objects between commands and has a far larger command set, while Command Prompt is the older, simpler batch-file shell
opts.D: PowerShell and Command Prompt are two names for exactly the same program

exp: PowerShell's cmdlets pass .NET objects along the pipeline instead of plain text, which is why it can do administrative work that batch files cannot. Command Prompt is retained mainly for compatibility with legacy batch scripts and is the effectively legacy option for new administrative scripting.

q: What does the Windows Registry contain?

opts.A: The installation files of every program on the computer
opts.B: A central hierarchical database of configuration settings for Windows, hardware, installed applications and user profiles
opts.C: A log of every web page visited from the computer
opts.D: The user's documents, pictures and other personal files

exp: The Registry is a settings database organised into hives and keys, replacing the scattered INI files used by very early Windows versions. It records configuration only; program files live in Program Files and personal data lives in the user's profile folders.

q: Why are users warned to be careful when editing the Windows Registry with Registry Editor?

opts.A: Every edit is automatically broadcast to the other computers on the network
opts.B: The Registry can be edited only once, after which it becomes permanently read-only
opts.C: Editing the Registry removes all installed applications from the computer
opts.D: An incorrect change can stop Windows or an installed application from working, so the affected keys should be exported or a restore point created before editing

exp: Registry Editor applies changes immediately with no undo and no validation, so a wrong value in a system key can leave Windows unbootable. Exporting the branch first, or creating a system restore point, gives you a way back.

q: In the layered architecture of a Linux system, which component interacts directly with the hardware and manages memory, processes and devices?

opts.A: The kernel
opts.B: The shell
opts.C: The desktop environment
opts.D: The package manager

exp: The kernel is the core layer sitting between the hardware and everything else, handling process scheduling, memory management and device drivers through its device-driver and system-call interfaces. The shell is only a user-level program that asks the kernel to do this work on the user's behalf.

q: What is the role of the shell, such as bash, in a Linux system?

opts.A: It stores the system's configuration files
opts.B: It provides the graphical desktop and window manager
opts.C: It interprets the commands the user types and passes the requests to the operating system for execution
opts.D: It allocates memory directly to running processes

exp: The shell is the command interpreter: it reads a command line, locates the program, and asks the kernel to run it, which is why it is described as the layer between the user and the kernel. Memory allocation is the kernel's responsibility, not the shell's.

q: In the standard Linux directory layout, which directory holds system-wide configuration files?

opts.A: /var
opts.B: /etc
opts.C: /home
opts.D: /bin

exp: By the Filesystem Hierarchy Standard, /etc is the location for host-specific configuration files. /var holds variable data such as logs and spool files, /home holds users' personal directories, and /bin holds essential command binaries.

q: How does the Linux file system differ from the way Windows presents storage to the user?

opts.A: Linux permits only one partition on each physical disk
opts.B: Linux keeps all files in a single flat directory with no subdirectories
opts.C: Linux uses drive letters such as C: and D: but allows no more than two of them
opts.D: Linux presents everything as one tree starting at the root directory /, with additional disks and partitions attached at mount points instead of being given drive letters

exp: Linux has a single rooted hierarchy: a second disk does not become a new lettered drive but appears as a directory such as /mnt/data once it is mounted. Linux supports multiple partitions and a full directory hierarchy just as Windows does; only the naming model differs.

q: Which Linux command displays the full path of the directory you are currently working in?

opts.A: pwd
opts.B: ls
opts.C: cd
opts.D: mkdir

exp: pwd stands for 'print working directory' and outputs the absolute path of your current location. ls lists the contents of a directory, cd changes to a different one, and mkdir creates a new one.

q: Which Linux command searches for lines containing a given text pattern inside a file?

opts.A: cat
opts.B: chmod
opts.C: grep
opts.D: mv

exp: grep scans its input and prints only the lines that match the pattern given, for example grep error logfile.txt. cat displays a whole file without filtering it, chmod changes file permissions, and mv moves or renames files.

q: What does it mean for software to be released under an open-source licence?

opts.A: The software is always written by unpaid volunteers and may never be sold commercially
opts.B: The source code is made available so that anyone may study, modify and redistribute it, subject to the conditions of the licence
opts.C: The software carries no licence at all and is therefore in the public domain
opts.D: The software may be used free of charge, but the source code remains with the vendor

exp: Open source is about the availability of the source code and the rights granted over it, not about price; open-source software is still copyrighted and still licensed, and it may be sold or supported commercially. Software that is free of charge but keeps its source closed is freeware, which is a different thing.

q: In the Linux world, what is a 'distribution' such as Ubuntu, Debian, Fedora or Red Hat Enterprise Linux?

opts.A: A complete packaged operating system that combines the Linux kernel with system tools, a package manager and a selected set of applications
opts.B: A separate kernel written from scratch by each vendor
opts.C: A licence that governs the terms on which Linux may be copied
opts.D: The mirror server from which the Linux source code is downloaded

exp: All distributions share the same Linux kernel; what distinguishes them is the packaging, the package manager, the default software selection, the release cadence and the support arrangement, which may be community-based as with Debian or vendor-backed with paid subscriptions as with Red Hat Enterprise Linux.

q: What is the essential difference between lossless and lossy compression?

opts.A: Lossless compression works only on text files and lossy compression only on numeric data
opts.B: Lossless compression always produces smaller files than lossy compression
opts.C: Lossy compression can be reversed exactly, whereas lossless compression cannot
opts.D: Lossless compression restores the original data exactly when decompressed, while lossy compression permanently discards some data in order to achieve a smaller size

exp: Lossless methods such as ZIP and PNG reconstruct the original bit for bit, which is essential for documents, programs and archives; lossy methods such as JPEG and MP3 throw away detail the eye or ear is unlikely to notice. Because it discards data, lossy compression normally achieves the smaller file, not the larger one.

q: A user adds a folder of JPEG photographs to a ZIP archive and finds the archive is barely smaller than the original folder. What is the most likely reason?

opts.A: ZIP archives can compress only plain text files
opts.B: The photographs must be encrypted before they can be compressed
opts.C: JPEG files are already compressed, so little redundancy remains for a general-purpose compressor to remove
opts.D: ZIP compresses only the file names and never the file contents

exp: Compression works by removing redundancy, and a JPEG has already had most of its redundancy squeezed out, so a second pass gains almost nothing. ZIP handles any file type, but it can only shrink data that still contains repetition.

q: A laptop's system drive is protected with BitLocker. What protection does this actually provide?

opts.A: It prevents viruses from running while Windows is loaded
opts.B: If the laptop is stolen and the drive is removed and connected to another machine, the data on it cannot be read without the correct credentials or the recovery key
opts.C: It stops other users of the same laptop from opening the owner's files after they have signed in with their own accounts
opts.D: It automatically uploads a copy of every file to OneDrive for safe keeping

exp: Full-volume encryption defends data at rest against physical theft of the disk; once Windows has unlocked the volume and the user has signed in, the files are readable as normal. Keeping one signed-in user out of another's files is the job of NTFS permissions and EFS, not BitLocker.

q: What is the main difference between the Encrypting File System (EFS) and BitLocker in Windows?

opts.A: EFS encrypts individual files and folders and ties them to a particular user account, while BitLocker encrypts an entire volume
opts.B: EFS encrypts entire volumes, while BitLocker encrypts only individual files
opts.C: EFS protects data while it travels over the network, while BitLocker protects data stored on disk
opts.D: EFS is a backup utility, while BitLocker is a compression utility

exp: EFS works at the level of the file or folder, using keys tied to a user's account so that other signed-in users cannot read the content; BitLocker works at the level of the whole volume and protects against the disk being removed. Neither protects data in transit, which is the role of protocols such as TLS.

q: What does an incremental backup copy?

opts.A: Every file on the system, on each occasion that it runs
opts.B: Only the files the user picks by hand at the time the backup runs
opts.C: All files changed since the last full backup, however many backup runs ago that was
opts.D: Only the files that have changed since the previous backup of any kind, whether that was a full or an incremental one

exp: An incremental backup measures change from the most recent backup of any type, which keeps each run small and fast but means a restore needs the full backup plus every incremental since. Option C describes a differential backup, which always measures from the last full backup and therefore grows larger each day.

q: Why should a test restore be carried out from backup media from time to time?

opts.A: Restoring compresses the backup so that it occupies less space
opts.B: A backup that is never restored expires and is deleted automatically
opts.C: It is the only way to confirm the backup is complete and readable, because a backup job can report success while producing media that cannot in fact be restored
opts.D: A test restore is required before an incremental backup can be converted into a full backup

exp: Media faults, silent job errors and incomplete file selections often surface only at restore time, so an untested backup is an assumption rather than a protection. This is why a recovery drill is treated as part of the backup process itself, alongside the practice of keeping copies on more than one medium and one of them off site.

q: A user has emptied the Recycle Bin and now needs an important file back. What is the most important immediate step to improve the chance of recovering it?

opts.A: Defragment the drive so the deleted file is moved back together
opts.B: Stop writing any new data to that drive and attempt recovery as soon as possible
opts.C: Format the drive and then run a file recovery program on it
opts.D: Run a full disk check with repair options on the drive first

exp: Deleting a file usually only marks its space as free; the data survives until something else is written over that space, so every further write reduces the chance of recovery. Defragmenting, formatting or running repair utilities all write to the drive and therefore make recovery less likely, not more.

q: Which Windows feature lets a user restore an earlier saved copy of a file or folder taken from a shadow copy or restore point?

opts.A: Recycle Bin
opts.B: Disk Cleanup
opts.C: Previous Versions
opts.D: Quick Format

exp: Previous Versions exposes older copies of a file or folder captured by shadow copies or restore points, so a file can be rolled back even if it was overwritten rather than deleted. The Recycle Bin only holds files that were deleted through Explorer and keeps just the one deleted copy, not a history of earlier versions.

q: A newly connected scanner is not working and the driver is suspected. Which tool is opened to check the device's status and update its driver?

opts.A: Device Manager
opts.B: Disk Management
opts.C: Event Viewer
opts.D: Resource Monitor

exp: Device Manager is the console that lists the hardware attached to the computer along with its drivers, and it is where drivers are updated, rolled back, disabled or uninstalled. Event Viewer may record that the device failed, but it cannot manage the driver itself.

q: In Device Manager, a device listed with a yellow warning marker beside it indicates that:

opts.A: The device has been switched off to save power
opts.B: The device is being shared with other users on the network
opts.C: The device is newer than the installed version of Windows
opts.D: The device has a problem, typically a missing or malfunctioning driver

exp: The yellow warning marker in Device Manager flags a device that Windows has detected but cannot use correctly, most often because its driver is missing, wrong or has failed to start. Power saving and network sharing are not shown by this marker at all.

q: A second hard disk has been fitted to a PC but does not appear in File Explorer. Which tool is used to bring it online, create a volume on it and assign a drive letter?

opts.A: Device Manager
opts.B: Task Manager
opts.C: Disk Management
opts.D: Services

exp: Disk Management is the console for disks, partitions and volumes, and it handles initialising a new disk, creating and formatting volumes, and assigning or changing drive letters. Device Manager would show that the disk hardware is present, but it cannot partition or format it.

q: In Disk Management, the ordinary default disk type used by Windows, which stores data in primary and logical partitions, is called a:

opts.A: Basic disk
opts.B: Dynamic disk
opts.C: Spanned volume
opts.D: Mounted folder

exp: A basic disk is the standard disk type, organised into ordinary partitions, and it is what a newly initialised disk becomes by default. A dynamic disk is the alternative type that must be converted to before advanced layouts such as spanned volumes can be created.

q: An application has stopped responding and will not close normally. Which tool gives the quickest way to force it to close?

opts.A: Event Viewer
opts.B: Disk Management
opts.C: Performance Monitor
opts.D: Task Manager

exp: Task Manager lists the running applications and processes and provides the End task option that terminates a hung program immediately. Event Viewer would only record the crash afterwards, and Performance Monitor merely collects measurements without controlling processes.

q: Which tab of Task Manager lists the programs configured to run automatically when Windows starts, and allows them to be disabled?

opts.A: Processes
opts.B: Startup
opts.C: Performance
opts.D: Details

exp: The Startup tab shows the programs that launch at sign-in together with their impact on boot time, and lets each one be enabled or disabled. The Processes and Details tabs list what is running at this moment, which is not the same as what is set to start later.

q: You must identify the single process causing continuous heavy disk activity, including the exact files it is reading and writing. Which tool provides this level of detail?

opts.A: Resource Monitor
opts.B: Task Manager
opts.C: Device Manager
opts.D: Event Viewer

exp: Resource Monitor drills down per process and per resource, listing the individual files a process is reading or writing and the network connections it holds. Task Manager will show that disk usage is high and which process is busiest, but it does not name the files involved.

q: Compared with Task Manager, what does Resource Monitor mainly add?

opts.A: It lists all installed hardware together with their driver versions
opts.B: It stores the System, Application and Security logs for later reading
opts.C: It breaks activity down per process, showing the files, handles and network connections each one is using
opts.D: It records counter readings to a log file for several weeks of trend analysis

exp: Resource Monitor sits between the quick summary of Task Manager and long-term logging, giving a detailed live breakdown of CPU, disk, network and memory activity attributed to individual processes. Listing hardware is Device Manager's job, storing logs is Event Viewer's, and long-term counter logging is what Performance Monitor is designed for.

q: A Windows computer restarted unexpectedly overnight with no explanation. Which tool should be checked first for recorded errors and shutdown messages from that time?

opts.A: Task Manager
opts.B: Event Viewer
opts.C: Disk Management
opts.D: Device Manager

exp: Event Viewer keeps the timestamped logs of errors, warnings and information messages raised by Windows and applications, so it is the standard first place to look after an unexplained failure. Task Manager only shows the present moment and keeps no history of what happened overnight.

q: In Event Viewer, failed logon attempts on a computer are recorded in which log?

opts.A: Application
opts.B: System
opts.C: Setup
opts.D: Security

exp: The Security log holds audit records such as successful and failed logon attempts and other access events, which makes it the log examined during a security investigation. The System log records events raised by Windows components and drivers, and the Application log records events raised by installed programs.

q: Which service startup type means the service will not run at all, and cannot even be started manually, until the setting is changed?

opts.A: Automatic
opts.B: Manual
opts.C: Disabled
opts.D: Automatic (Delayed Start)

exp: Disabled blocks the service from starting by any means until an administrator changes the startup type back. Manual is the type that keeps the service stopped at boot but still allows it to be started on demand, which is the distinction being tested.

q: In Windows, a service is best described as:

opts.A: A program that runs in the background, usually with no user interface, and can start automatically when the computer boots
opts.B: A shortcut that a user has placed in the Startup folder
opts.C: A driver file supplied by a hardware manufacturer
opts.D: A batch file that has been scheduled to run once each day

exp: Services are long-running background programs, such as the print spooler or a database engine, that present no window and are usually configured to start with the operating system rather than with a user session. A shortcut in the Startup folder runs only after a particular user logs on and is an ordinary application, not a service.

q: An administrator wants to collect CPU, memory and disk counter readings continuously for two weeks in order to establish a baseline. Which tool is designed for this?

opts.A: Task Manager
opts.B: Resource Monitor
opts.C: Event Viewer
opts.D: Performance Monitor

exp: Performance Monitor selects specific counters and logs their values over time, which is what makes long-term trend analysis and baselining possible. Task Manager and Resource Monitor both display live activity and are not intended to record weeks of data for later comparison.

q: Why does an administrator record a performance baseline for a server?

opts.A: To free disk space by removing old log files automatically
opts.B: To know what the normal readings are, so that later abnormal figures can be recognised
opts.C: To install any missing device drivers without user intervention
opts.D: To restore files that were deleted from the Recycle Bin

exp: A baseline is a record of how the system behaves under normal conditions, and without it a later reading such as 70 per cent memory use cannot be judged as acceptable or alarming. Baselining measures the system; it neither cleans up disk space nor changes any configuration.

q: PowerShell commands are called cmdlets and follow a standard naming pattern. Which pattern is it?

opts.A: Verb-Noun, such as Get-Process
opts.B: Noun-Verb, such as Process-Get
opts.C: An abbreviation of the full command, such as gtprc
opts.D: A verb on its own, such as Get

exp: Every cmdlet is named as an approved verb followed by a hyphen and a singular noun, giving predictable names such as Get-Process, Get-Service and Stop-Service. This consistency lets an administrator guess a command's name from what it does, which is one of PowerShell's design goals.

q: What is the key difference between the PowerShell pipeline and the Command Prompt pipeline?

opts.A: PowerShell can run only one command at a time, so it has no pipeline
opts.B: Command Prompt passes objects between commands while PowerShell passes plain text
opts.C: PowerShell passes structured objects between commands, while Command Prompt passes plain text
opts.D: Both pass plain text, but PowerShell shows it in colour

exp: In PowerShell the output of one cmdlet is a set of objects with named properties, so the next cmdlet can filter or sort on those properties directly. Command Prompt pipes only a stream of characters, which is why text there has to be parsed with tools such as find before it can be used.

q: A simple script containing a list of Windows commands that are run one after another is traditionally saved with which file extension?

opts.A: .exe
opts.B: .bat
opts.C: .ps1
opts.D: .txt

exp: A batch file is a plain text file of commands saved with the .bat extension, which the command interpreter then executes line by line. The .ps1 extension belongs to PowerShell scripts and .exe is a compiled program, neither of which is a batch file.

q: In a batch file, what is the effect of placing @ECHO OFF on the first line?

opts.A: All output produced by the batch file is suppressed
opts.B: The batch file stops running at the first command that fails
opts.C: The batch file is run with administrator rights
opts.D: The commands themselves are not displayed on screen as the file runs

exp: ECHO OFF stops the interpreter from printing each command before executing it, and the leading @ hides that line itself, giving clean output. The commands still run and their own output still appears, so this is not the same as suppressing all output.

q: An office wants every circular it issues to open with the same letterhead, margins, fonts and heading layout. Which Word feature is designed for this?

opts.A: Mail Merge
opts.B: A document template
opts.C: A section break
opts.D: An AutoCorrect entry

exp: A template is a reusable starting document that already carries the required page setup, styles and boilerplate, so every new circular begins identically. Mail Merge is for producing many copies of one letter with different names and addresses, which is a different problem.

q: A clerk creates a new document from the office's standard template, edits it heavily and saves it under a new name. What happens to the template file itself?

opts.A: The template is updated to include all the edits
opts.B: The template is locked and cannot be used again
opts.C: The template is unchanged; the new document is a separate copy
opts.D: The template is replaced by the newly saved document

exp: Creating a document from a template copies the template's content and formatting into a fresh document, leaving the template untouched. To change the office standard you must open and edit the template file itself, not a document made from it.

q: In Word, SmartArt is used to

opts.A: insert a ready-made diagram such as a process, cycle, hierarchy or relationship graphic
opts.B: apply artistic effects and corrections to a photograph
opts.C: plot a graph from a table of numeric data
opts.D: convert a document into a web page

exp: SmartArt supplies pre-designed diagram layouts — lists, processes, cycles, hierarchies and relationship graphics — into which you type text. Plotting numeric data is the job of a chart, which is a separate feature.

q: A note already contains a typed bulleted list of five approval steps, and the officer wants it shown as a process diagram. What is the quickest way in Word?

opts.A: Draw each box and arrow manually using shapes and text boxes
opts.B: Insert each step as separate WordArt text
opts.C: Take a screenshot of the list and insert it as a picture
opts.D: Select the list and convert it to a SmartArt graphic

exp: Word can convert selected list text directly into a SmartArt graphic, placing each bullet into a shape of the chosen layout, and the text stays editable afterwards. Drawing the shapes by hand gives the same look but is slow and the result is not linked to the list text.

q: A long report contains the sentence "see Table 4 on page 12". Which Word feature keeps that pointer correct if another table is inserted earlier and the numbering and pagination shift?

opts.A: A footnote placed at that point
opts.B: A cross-reference to the numbered table caption
opts.C: A hyperlink to an external website
opts.D: Typing the number in bold so it is easy to spot later

exp: A cross-reference is a field that points at a captioned item, so when the document is updated it re-reads the item's current number and page. Text typed by hand, however it is formatted, does not change when the document does.

q: In Word, a footnote is

opts.A: a note printed at the bottom of the same page as its reference mark
opts.B: a note collected at the end of the whole document
opts.C: text that repeats at the bottom of every page, such as a page number
opts.D: a remark visible only to reviewers and never printed

exp: A footnote sits at the foot of the page carrying its reference mark, and Word renumbers footnotes automatically as they are added or removed. A note gathered at the end of the document is an endnote, and repeating text at the bottom of every page is the footer.

q: Word's automatic Table of Contents is generated from

opts.A: bookmarks the user inserts at each section
opts.B: any text that has been made bold and given a larger font size
opts.C: the heading styles applied to the document's headings
opts.D: the page numbers placed in the header or footer

exp: Word collects the text of paragraphs formatted with heading styles and builds the contents list from them, with the style level deciding the indent level. A heading merely made bold and enlarged carries no style, so Word cannot see it and it will be left out.

q: New sections have been added to a report, so the headings and page numbers have changed but the automatic Table of Contents still shows the old ones. What should be done?

opts.A: Retype the contents page by hand to match
opts.B: Nothing — the contents list always changes as you type
opts.C: Convert the contents list to a table before it will refresh
opts.D: Update the Table of Contents so it re-reads the headings and page numbers

exp: An automatic Table of Contents is a field, and a field shows the values captured when it was last built, so it must be updated to pick up new headings and changed pagination. It does not refresh continuously while you type, which is exactly why documents are so often issued with a stale contents page.

q: In Word, what is the relationship between the citations inserted in the text and the bibliography at the end?

opts.A: Word builds the bibliography automatically from the sources cited in the document
opts.B: The bibliography must be typed separately and has no link to the citations
opts.C: The bibliography is generated from the document's heading styles
opts.D: A bibliography can only be created if the document already has a table of contents

exp: Each citation is attached to a stored source record, and the bibliography is generated from those records, so adding a citation adds its source to the list. Typing the list by hand defeats the feature and lets the text and the list drift apart.

q: In Word's citation tools, APA, MLA and Chicago are examples of

opts.A: file formats in which a document can be saved
opts.B: citation styles that decide how references are formatted
opts.C: built-in font and colour schemes
opts.D: proofing languages for the spelling checker

exp: A citation style is a set of formatting conventions for references, and selecting one reformats every citation and the whole bibliography consistently. They control presentation of sources only; they have nothing to do with how the file is saved.

q: With Track Changes turned on, what happens when a reviewer deletes a sentence from the document?

opts.A: The sentence is removed permanently and at once
opts.B: The sentence is moved to the clipboard for later use
opts.C: The deletion is recorded as a revision that can later be accepted or rejected
opts.D: The sentence is automatically copied into a comment

exp: Track Changes records every insertion, deletion and formatting change as a revision mark, so the author can go through them one by one and accept or reject each. The text only really goes when the deletion is accepted.

q: Why should an official Word document be checked for remaining tracked changes and comments before it is sent outside the office?

opts.A: Because unaccepted revisions and comments stay in the file and can expose internal drafting to the recipient
opts.B: Because comments prevent the file from being opened on another computer
opts.C: Because tracked changes stop the document from being printed
opts.D: Because revision marks increase the file size beyond the e-mail limit

exp: Revisions and comments are stored inside the file, so a recipient can display them and read internal remarks and rejected wording — a real risk in official correspondence. Accepting or rejecting all changes and removing comments before issue is the standard precaution.

q: The main purpose of adding alternative text (alt text) to a picture in a document is to

opts.A: give a description that a screen reader can read out to a visually impaired user
opts.B: reduce the file size of the picture
opts.C: make the picture print more sharply
opts.D: lock the picture so it cannot be moved

exp: Alt text carries the meaning of an image in words, so assistive software can convey it to a reader who cannot see the picture. It affects accessibility only, not the image's size, print quality or position.

q: Which of the following makes an official document more accessible?

opts.A: Marking section titles by making them large and bold by hand
opts.B: Writing every link as "click here"
opts.C: Applying the built-in heading styles so the document has a real navigable structure
opts.D: Using colour alone to show which paragraphs are important

exp: Heading styles give the document a structure that screen readers can announce and navigate, which text merely made bold and large does not. Word's Accessibility Checker flags exactly these problems — missing headings, vague link text and reliance on colour — before the document is issued.

q: Two officers in different sections must work on the same Word document at the same time and always see each other's latest text. What makes this possible?

opts.A: E-mailing the document back and forth as an attachment
opts.B: Storing the file in OneDrive or SharePoint and co-authoring it in Word
opts.C: Each keeping a copy on a pen drive and merging at the end
opts.D: Turning on Track Changes in two separate local copies

exp: Co-authoring works because the file lives in cloud storage, so both people open the one copy and edits are synchronised as they type. Attachments and pen drives create separate copies that immediately diverge and then have to be reconciled by hand.

q: What is the main benefit of version history for a document stored in OneDrive or SharePoint?

opts.A: It keeps several files with different names in the same folder
opts.B: It compresses the document a little more at every save
opts.C: It prevents anyone other than the author from editing the document
opts.D: It keeps earlier versions of the file so an older one can be viewed or restored

exp: Version history stores successive saved states of the same file, so a wrong or unwanted edit can be undone by restoring an earlier version. It records changes rather than restricting who may edit, which is the separate job of sharing permissions.

q: A draft letter has been prepared in Word and now needs the approval of a senior officer through eOffice. What is the normal way to do this?

opts.A: Upload the draft into the relevant electronic file as a draft for approval so it moves up the hierarchy
opts.B: Paste the text into a personal e-mail to the officer
opts.C: Keep the file on the local desktop and inform the officer verbally
opts.D: Share the file through a public file-sharing website

exp: In eOffice the draft is attached to the electronic file and routed for approval, so the noting, the approval and the audit trail all stay inside the system. Sending the text by personal e-mail or a public link leaves no official record and takes departmental content outside the government network.

q: Why is a finalised Word document usually converted to PDF before it is issued or placed on record in eOffice?

opts.A: Because PDF files can be edited more easily than Word files
opts.B: Because a Word file cannot be uploaded to eOffice at all
opts.C: Because PDF fixes the layout across different computers and gives a stable record that can carry a digital signature
opts.D: Because spelling and grammar can only be checked in PDF

exp: PDF preserves fonts, pagination and layout wherever it is opened and is the usual format for a signed, final record, so what is signed is exactly what the recipient sees. Being harder to alter than an editable Word file is a reason for using it, not against it.

q: In concept, what does an AI writing assistant such as Microsoft Copilot do inside a word processor?

opts.A: It replaces the need for any human review, because its output is always factually correct
opts.B: It helps draft, summarise and rewrite text, which the user must still read, verify and edit
opts.C: It converts documents into spreadsheets and databases
opts.D: It only corrects spelling and grammar mistakes

exp: An AI assistant produces suggested drafts, summaries and rewordings from a user's instruction, and responsibility for accuracy stays with the officer who signs the document. It goes well beyond a spelling checker, but its output can be wrong or invented and therefore always needs checking.

q: An official wants to paste the text of an internal office note into a public AI chat service to have it reworded. What is the main concern?

opts.A: The reply may come back in a different font
opts.B: The document will lose its page numbering
opts.C: AI tools are unable to produce formal language
opts.D: Confidential and personal data would leave departmental control and may be retained by the service

exp: Anything pasted into a public AI service is sent to an outside provider and may be stored there, so official records and personal data must not be put into one. Formatting problems are trivial by comparison and easily fixed after the text is brought back.

q: In a VLOOKUP formula, what is the effect of setting the last argument (range_lookup) to FALSE or 0?

opts.A: The function searches from right to left across the table
opts.B: The function returns a result only for an exact match, and #N/A if none is found
opts.C: The function returns the closest smaller value when no exact match exists
opts.D: The function returns the whole matching row instead of a single value

exp: FALSE (or 0) asks VLOOKUP for an exact match, so an unmatched lookup value produces #N/A rather than a wrong answer. TRUE (or 1, or omitting the argument) is the approximate match, which returns the nearest lower value and requires the first column to be sorted in ascending order.

q: Why do experienced users often prefer INDEX together with MATCH instead of VLOOKUP?

opts.A: VLOOKUP cannot be used on text values, only on numbers
opts.B: VLOOKUP can only be used within a single worksheet
opts.C: VLOOKUP can only return a value from a column to the right of the lookup column, while INDEX with MATCH can fetch a value on either side
opts.D: VLOOKUP always requires the lookup table to be converted into a chart first

exp: VLOOKUP searches the leftmost column of its table and can only return a value from a column further right, so it fails when the required value sits to the left of the key. INDEX with MATCH separates the search from the retrieval, so the returned column may lie on either side; VLOOKUP handles text perfectly well and can refer to other sheets, so those are not the reason.

q: Which Excel function calculates the fixed periodic instalment payable on a loan taken at a constant interest rate for a fixed number of periods?

opts.A: PMT
opts.B: NPER
opts.C: RATE
opts.D: FV

exp: PMT returns the constant payment for each period of a loan or investment. NPER returns how many periods are needed, RATE returns the interest rate per period, and FV returns the accumulated future value, so none of them gives the instalment amount.

q: What does the PV function in Excel return?

opts.A: The number of payment periods in a loan or investment
opts.B: The interest rate charged for each period
opts.C: The value an investment will grow to at the end of the term
opts.D: The amount that a series of future payments is worth in today's money at a given interest rate

exp: PV stands for present value and discounts a stream of future payments back to what it is worth now at the stated rate per period. The value at the end of the term is what FV returns, while NPER and RATE give the number of periods and the periodic rate respectively.

q: A department wants its data-entry operators to be able to enter only approved district names in a column, chosen from a fixed list. Which Excel feature enforces this?

opts.A: Conditional Formatting
opts.B: Data Validation with the List criterion
opts.C: Protect Workbook
opts.D: Text to Columns

exp: Data Validation with the List criterion attaches a drop-down of permitted entries to the cells and rejects anything outside that list, which is exactly how data-entry is constrained to valid values. Conditional Formatting can only colour a wrong entry after it has been typed; it cannot prevent it.

q: In the Data Validation dialog box, what does the Input Message do?

opts.A: It shows a small note as soon as the cell is selected, telling the user what may be entered
opts.B: It appears only after an invalid value has been typed and stops the entry
opts.C: It draws red circles around cells that already contain invalid values
opts.D: It records the name of the user who entered each value

exp: The Input Message is a prompt that pops up when the cell is selected, so it guides the operator before anything is typed. The message that appears after a wrong entry and blocks or warns about it is the Error Alert, which is a separate tab in the same dialog box.

q: A clerk selects only the Name column of an employee table, sorts it A to Z and chooses to continue with the current selection. What is the result?

opts.A: The entire table is rearranged so each row stays with its own name
opts.B: Excel refuses to sort because the selection is incomplete
opts.C: Only the names are reordered, so each name is now lined up against another employee's details
opts.D: The remaining columns are cleared and must be re-entered

exp: Sorting a single selected column moves only that column's values while every other column stays where it is, silently breaking the link between each record's fields. Choosing to expand the selection instead keeps whole rows together, which is why that option should always be taken on a table of records.

q: Which capability does Advanced Filter provide that AutoFilter does not?

opts.A: Applying criteria to more than one column of the list
opts.B: Temporarily hiding the rows that do not match the criteria
opts.C: Filtering columns that contain text rather than numbers
opts.D: Using a separate criteria range on the sheet and copying the matching rows to another location

exp: Advanced Filter reads its conditions from a criteria range written on the worksheet and can extract the matching rows to a different area instead of merely hiding the rest. AutoFilter already handles several columns, text values and hiding non-matching rows, so those are not the distinguishing features.

q: An officer has a list of several thousand expenditure records and needs district-wise totals of the amounts. Which Excel feature produces this summary without writing any formulas?

opts.A: PivotTable
opts.B: Advanced Filter
opts.C: Conditional Formatting
opts.D: Goal Seek

exp: A PivotTable groups a long list by a chosen field and aggregates the numeric fields automatically, so district-wise totals appear by dragging District into the Rows area and Amount into the Values area. Advanced Filter can only select rows that meet criteria; it does not aggregate them.

q: Several values in the source data of an existing pivot table are corrected. What must be done for the pivot table to display the corrected totals?

opts.A: Nothing, because a pivot table always reflects its source data instantly
opts.B: The pivot table must be refreshed
opts.C: The pivot table must be deleted and built again from scratch
opts.D: The source data must be sorted before the pivot table will recalculate

exp: A pivot table works from a cached copy of the source data, so edits to the source appear only after a refresh. It does not update live the way an ordinary formula does, but it also does not need to be rebuilt, since Refresh re-reads the same source range.

q: In Excel, a dashboard is best described as

opts.A: a worksheet holding the raw transaction records for the whole year
opts.B: a protected worksheet in which no cell can be edited
opts.C: a template that fixes the page layout used for printing
opts.D: a single view that brings together the key figures of a dataset using pivot tables, charts and other summary elements

exp: A dashboard is a consolidated summary screen, usually built from pivot tables and charts driven by data held on other sheets, so a reader sees the important numbers at a glance. The raw records normally sit on a separate data sheet that feeds the dashboard rather than on the dashboard itself.

q: On an Excel dashboard, what is the purpose of a slicer?

opts.A: It keeps the heading rows visible while the sheet is scrolled
opts.B: It converts a chart into a static picture so it cannot change
opts.C: It provides clickable buttons that filter the pivot tables and charts connected to it
opts.D: It recalculates every formula in the workbook when clicked

exp: A slicer is a visual filter: each button represents a value of a field, and clicking it filters every pivot table or chart the slicer is connected to, which is what makes a dashboard interactive. Keeping headings on screen while scrolling is done with Freeze Panes instead.

q: Which Excel tool finds the value that must be placed in one input cell so that a formula in another cell reaches a specified result?

opts.A: Goal Seek
opts.B: Scenario Manager
opts.C: Conditional Formatting
opts.D: Data Validation

exp: Goal Seek works backwards from a desired formula result to the input value that produces it, for example finding the sales figure needed to reach a target profit. Scenario Manager only stores and displays sets of input values that the user supplies; it does not solve for one.

q: What is the main limitation of Goal Seek compared with Solver?

opts.A: Goal Seek cannot be used on formulas that refer to other cells
opts.B: Goal Seek can adjust only one input cell and cannot apply constraints
opts.C: Goal Seek works only on whole numbers
opts.D: Goal Seek requires the worksheet to be sorted before it will run

exp: Goal Seek changes a single variable cell to hit one target value and accepts no additional conditions, whereas Solver can vary several cells at once and honour constraints while maximising, minimising or targeting a result. Goal Seek needs a formula referring to the changing cell in order to work at all, so that is a requirement rather than a limitation.

q: What is the main purpose of Power Query in Excel?

opts.A: To summarise a table by dragging fields into rows, columns and values areas
opts.B: To store recorded keystrokes as VBA code for later replay
opts.C: To connect to external data sources and clean and reshape the data before it is loaded into the workbook
opts.D: To protect a workbook so that only authorised users can open it

exp: Power Query is the get-and-transform layer of Excel: it imports data from files, databases and other sources and lets the user remove, split, filter and reshape columns before loading the tidied result. Summarising with rows, columns and values areas is what a pivot table does after the data has been loaded.

q: A user builds a Power Query that removes blank rows and splits a column, then loads the result. The source file is later updated with new records. What happens when the query is refreshed?
