opts.A: The saved transformation steps are applied again automatically to the updated data
opts.B: The transformations have to be carried out by hand each time the data changes
opts.C: Refreshing reloads the raw data and discards all the steps that were applied
opts.D: A second copy of the untransformed data is added beside the existing result

exp: Power Query records each transformation as a step in the query, so a refresh re-runs the whole sequence against the current source data, which is why it suits reports that must be produced repeatedly. This repeatability is the main advantage over cleaning the data manually every month.

q: Power Pivot extends Excel mainly by allowing the user to

opts.A: import a table from a web page into a worksheet
opts.B: automate repetitive formatting by recording the steps taken
opts.C: work backwards from a target result to the input value that produces it
opts.D: build a data model of several related tables and analyse them together

exp: Power Pivot holds a data model in which multiple tables are linked by relationships, so figures can be summarised across tables without pulling everything into one sheet with lookup formulas, and it copes with far larger datasets than a plain worksheet. Importing and cleaning the data is Power Query's job; Power Pivot is what models and analyses it afterwards.

q: Which formula language is used to write calculated columns and measures in a Power Pivot data model?

opts.A: VBA
opts.B: DAX
opts.C: SQL
opts.D: HTML

exp: DAX, short for Data Analysis Expressions, is the language of calculated columns and measures in the Power Pivot data model. VBA is the language behind Excel macros and is not used for data-model calculations.

q: A workbook containing recorded macros must be saved in which file format if the macros are to be kept?

opts.A: .xlsx
opts.B: .csv
opts.C: .xlsm
opts.D: .xltx

exp: .xlsm is the macro-enabled workbook format and is the one that stores the VBA code along with the sheets. Saving the same workbook as .xlsx discards the macros, because the ordinary workbook format is defined not to carry executable code.

q: Why does Excel disable macros by default in a workbook received by e-mail or downloaded from the internet?

opts.A: Because macros make the file too large to open quickly
opts.B: Because macros run only in the exact version of Excel that created them
opts.C: Because a workbook containing macros cannot be shared with other users
opts.D: Because macro code can perform harmful actions on the computer, so macros from an untrusted source are a security risk

exp: A macro is program code stored inside the file, and malicious macros are a well-known way of delivering malware, so Excel blocks them until the user confirms the source is trusted. File size and version compatibility are not the reason for the warning.

q: Two officers need to work on the same Excel workbook at the same time and see each other's changes as they are made. Which Microsoft 365 capability makes this possible?

opts.A: Co-authoring on a workbook stored in OneDrive or SharePoint
opts.B: Sending the workbook to each officer as an e-mail attachment
opts.C: Protecting the worksheet with a password before editing
opts.D: Keeping separate copies and merging them at the end of the day

exp: Co-authoring requires the workbook to live in cloud storage such as OneDrive or SharePoint, after which several users can edit it simultaneously and see one another's changes and cell selections. Mailing attachments or keeping separate copies produces exactly the divergent versions that co-authoring is meant to avoid.

q: A shared Microsoft 365 workbook has been changed wrongly and the mistake is noticed only the next day. Which feature allows an earlier saved state of the file to be examined and restored?

opts.A: AutoRecover
opts.B: Version History
opts.C: Undo
opts.D: Freeze Panes

exp: Version History keeps earlier saved versions of a file held in OneDrive or SharePoint, so an older version can be opened, compared and restored long after the editing session has ended. Undo only reverses actions within the current session and is lost once the workbook is closed.

q: Which of the following best describes what an AI assistant built into a modern spreadsheet is designed to do?

opts.A: Guarantee that the data contains no errors before any analysis is done
opts.B: Remove the need to save or back up the workbook
opts.C: Describe trends in a selected range in plain language and suggest suitable formulas or charts
opts.D: Convert the workbook automatically into a relational database with enforced keys

exp: Spreadsheet AI assistants take a natural-language question about a range and answer it by summarising the data, pointing out patterns and proposing formulas or charts the user can accept. They work on the data as given and cannot certify that it is accurate, so any suggested formula still has to be checked by the user before it is relied on.

q: A government department wants to paste a spreadsheet of citizens' personal details into a free public AI chat service to get a quick analysis. What is the main objection to this?

opts.A: Official personal data would be sent outside government control to a third party, which breaches data protection and confidentiality obligations
opts.B: Public AI services are unable to read data that is arranged in rows and columns
opts.C: The workbook would permanently lose its formulas once the data was pasted
opts.D: The analysis would take longer than doing the same work by hand

exp: Pasting official records into a public AI service transfers personal data to an outside provider that may retain or process it, which conflicts with the department's duty to keep such data confidential and within approved systems. The technical objections are not the issue, since such services can read tabular data perfectly well; the problem is where the data ends up.

q: A slide must show the five stages a file passes through in an office, one after another from receipt to disposal. Which SmartArt layout category is designed for this?

opts.A: Cycle
opts.B: Hierarchy
opts.C: Process
opts.D: Relationship

exp: Process layouts show steps moving in one direction from a beginning to an end, which is exactly a start-to-finish workflow. Cycle is the tempting alternative, but it is meant for stages that return to the beginning and repeat, which a receipt-to-disposal sequence does not.

q: A slide contains a text placeholder with six bullet points. What does the 'Convert to SmartArt' option do to it?

opts.A: It keeps the bullet text and places each point inside a shape of the chosen diagram
opts.B: It deletes the bullets and inserts an empty diagram for the user to fill in
opts.C: It turns the bullets into a chart whose bars are sized by the length of each line
opts.D: It moves the bullets into the notes pane and puts a picture on the slide instead

exp: Converting to SmartArt reuses the existing bullet text as the labels of the diagram's shapes, so a wall of bullets becomes a visual that shows how the points relate. The text is not discarded, and the conversion is reversible back to a bulleted list.

q: A slide has to show how a department's annual budget is divided among its four heads of expenditure. Which chart type suits this best?

opts.A: Line chart
opts.B: Pie chart
opts.C: Scatter (XY) chart
opts.D: Stacked area chart

exp: A pie chart shows parts of a single whole, so each head appears as its share of the total budget. Line and area charts are built to show movement over time, which is not what a one-year split of a total is about.

q: A chart was copied from an Excel workbook and pasted into a slide with the option that links the data to the workbook. A figure in the workbook is later corrected. What can be said about the chart on the slide?

opts.A: It can never change, because a pasted chart becomes a picture
opts.B: Its colours will change but its plotted values will not
opts.C: The whole presentation must be made again to show the new figure
opts.D: It can be refreshed to show the corrected figure, because it is linked to the workbook

exp: A linked chart keeps a connection to its source workbook, so updating the link brings the corrected data onto the slide. Pasting as a picture is a different choice and is the one that freezes the chart permanently.

q: A video plays correctly in a presentation on the computer where the slides were made, but will not play when only the presentation file is copied to another laptop. What is the most likely reason?

opts.A: The video was linked to a file on the original computer instead of being embedded in the presentation
opts.B: Video can be played only from Presenter View
opts.C: Copying a presentation turns all of its videos into still images
opts.D: The video's playback was set to 'On Click' instead of 'Automatically'

exp: A linked video is not stored inside the presentation, only pointed to, so the link breaks when the file travels without the media; embedding stores the video in the file itself and avoids this. A playback setting of 'On Click' would still play the video when clicked, so it does not explain a video that will not play at all.

q: An audio clip inserted on the first slide is set to 'Play across slides'. What does this setting do?

opts.A: It copies the audio file onto every slide of the presentation
opts.B: It plays the audio only for as long as the first slide is on screen
opts.C: It lets the audio keep playing as the show moves on to the following slides
opts.D: It adds an audio icon to the printed handout of every slide

exp: 'Play across slides' allows one clip to continue over slide changes, which is how background music is set up for a show. Stopping when the slide changes is the default behaviour that this option is chosen to override.

q: A presentation is being delivered with Presenter View in use on a laptop connected to a projector. What does the audience see on the projected screen?

opts.A: The current slide together with the speaker's notes
opts.B: Only the current slide, filling the screen
opts.C: The current slide, the next slide and a timer
opts.D: A grid of thumbnails of all the slides

exp: Presenter View splits the two displays: the audience screen carries only the slide, while the extra information is kept on the presenter's own screen. Notes, the next slide and the timer are exactly the items that stay private to the speaker.

q: Which of the following appears on the presenter's own screen in Presenter View but is not shown to the audience?

opts.A: The animations applied to the current slide
opts.B: The design theme used by the presentation
opts.C: The pictures placed on the current slide
opts.D: The speaker notes for the current slide and the time elapsed

exp: Speaker notes, the elapsed-time clock, a timer and a preview of the next slide are the presenter-only part of Presenter View. Animations, the theme and the pictures are part of the slide itself and are therefore seen by the audience.

q: A presentation must run on its own at an exhibition stall, speaking its commentary and changing slides with nobody operating it. Which combination makes this possible?

opts.A: Recorded narration together with recorded slide timings
opts.B: Presenter View together with a second monitor
opts.C: Transitions set to 'On Click' together with a printed handout
opts.D: Comments on every slide together with edit permission for viewers

exp: Recording a presentation captures narration slide by slide and stores how long each slide was displayed, so the show can then advance and speak by itself. Presenter View is the opposite situation, since it assumes a live speaker standing at the machine.

q: A recorded presentation is exported as a video file. What does the resulting video contain?

opts.A: The slide images only, with no sound
opts.B: The recorded narration only, as an audio track
opts.C: The slides advancing on their recorded timings, along with the recorded narration
opts.D: An editable copy of the slides that the viewer can change

exp: Exporting to video turns the recorded show into a single playable file that carries both the timed slide sequence and the narration, so it can be watched without PowerPoint. A video is a finished playback file, not an editable copy of the slides.

q: Two officers open the same presentation stored in a shared cloud location and work on different slides at the same time, each seeing the other's changes appear. This way of working is called

opts.A: version history
opts.B: co-authoring
opts.C: Presenter View
opts.D: exporting to PDF

exp: Co-authoring is several people editing one cloud-stored file at the same time, with each person's edits visible to the others. Version history is a related collaboration feature but it looks backwards at earlier saved copies rather than allowing simultaneous editing.

q: What is the purpose of version history for a presentation kept in a shared cloud location?

opts.A: It counts how many times the slide show has been presented
opts.B: It lists everyone who has opened the file, without recording their changes
opts.C: It saves each slide as a separate file so slides can be reused elsewhere
opts.D: It lets an earlier saved version of the file be opened and restored

exp: Version history keeps earlier saved states of the file so that wording removed in later editing can be recovered, which matters when several people are editing the same deck. It is about the content of past versions, not merely a record of who opened the file.

q: Why is alternative text (alt text) added to a photograph or a chart on a slide?

opts.A: So that a screen reader can describe the image to a person who cannot see it
opts.B: So that the image is compressed to reduce the size of the file
opts.C: So that the image appears in the handout but not on the projected slide
opts.D: So that the image is automatically translated into another language

exp: Alt text is a short written description that assistive software reads out in place of the image, which is why accessible government presentations are expected to carry it on every meaningful picture and chart. It has nothing to do with compression, since file size is controlled separately.

q: Why does the reading order of the objects on a slide matter for accessibility?

opts.A: It fixes the order in which the objects are printed in the handout
opts.B: It sets the sequence in which animations play for the audience
opts.C: A screen reader announces the slide's items in that order, so a wrong order makes the slide confusing to follow
opts.D: It controls the order in which the slides advance during the show

exp: Assistive software works through a slide object by object in its stored reading order, so a title read after the body text leaves a listener without context. Animation order is a separate setting and changing it does not correct the order in which a screen reader reads the slide.

q: In an AI-assisted presentation tool, what is meant by generating a deck from an outline?

opts.A: The outline is printed as speaker notes for the person delivering the talk
opts.B: The tool produces a draft set of slides, with headings and suggested layouts, from the topics the user supplies
opts.C: The finished slides are converted back into a plain text outline for editing
opts.D: The finished slides are checked for spelling and grammar mistakes

exp: The assistant takes a short description or list of topics and drafts the slides, headings and layout suggestions, which the author then edits. Turning slides back into an outline is the reverse operation and is a long-standing feature unrelated to AI generation.

q: An officer plans to use a public AI assistant to help prepare a presentation on a departmental scheme. Which practice is correct?

opts.A: Paste the full list of beneficiaries with their details so that the draft is accurate
opts.B: Treat the generated slides as final, since AI output does not need checking
opts.C: Upload the internal note marked confidential, because AI services are private by default
opts.D: Keep confidential and personal data out of the public service, and verify the generated content before using it

exp: Official records and personal data should not be entered into a public AI service, and anything it produces is a draft that must be checked for accuracy before it goes out in a government presentation. Assuming such a service is private by default is unsafe, because the data leaves the department's control once it is pasted in.

q: A network is subnetted using a /26 prefix. How many usable host addresses does each resulting subnet contain?
exp: A /26 leaves 6 host bits, so each subnet holds 2^6 = 64 addresses, of which the all-zeros network address and the all-ones broadcast address cannot be assigned, giving 62 usable hosts. 64 is the total block size, not the usable count - subtract 2 whenever the question asks for hosts.

q: How does a host decide whether a destination IP address lies on its own local network or must be sent to the default gateway?

opts.A: It compares the first octet of the destination address with its own to identify the address class
opts.B: It performs a bitwise AND of the destination address with its own subnet mask and compares the result with its own network address
opts.C: It broadcasts an ARP request to every router until one replies
opts.D: It looks the destination up in its DNS cache to see if the name is local

exp: The subnet mask is 32 bits of contiguous 1s over the network portion, and ANDing an address with it yields the network address; if the destination's network address matches the host's own, delivery is direct on the LAN, otherwise the packet goes to the default gateway. Address class is irrelevant here - subnetting moves the network/host boundary away from the classful position.

q: Which statement correctly distinguishes switching from routing?

opts.A: Switching forwards frames at Layer 2 using MAC addresses; routing forwards packets at Layer 3 using IP addresses
opts.B: Switching forwards packets at Layer 3 using IP addresses; routing forwards frames at Layer 2 using MAC addresses
opts.C: Both use MAC addresses; switching is simply the faster of the two operations
opts.D: Switching consults a routing table while routing consults a MAC address table

exp: The OSI layer and the address type are what separate the two: a switch reads MAC addresses from its MAC (CAM) table at the Data Link layer, while a router reads destination IP addresses from its routing table at the Network layer. Speed or the physical size of the device has nothing to do with the distinction.

q: A PC sends a broadcast frame onto the LAN. Which device will stop that broadcast from going any further?

opts.A: A hub
opts.B: A Layer-2 switch in its default configuration
opts.C: A repeater
opts.D: A router

exp: Routers do not forward broadcasts, so each router interface bounds a separate broadcast domain. A switch breaks up collision domains but keeps all its ports in one broadcast domain unless VLANs are configured, and hubs and repeaters simply pass everything on.

q: What does a switch do with a frame whose destination MAC address is not yet in its MAC address table?

opts.A: It discards the frame and sends an error back to the sender
opts.B: It floods the frame out of every port except the one it arrived on
opts.C: It forwards the frame to the default gateway for routing
opts.D: It holds the frame until an administrator adds a static entry

exp: Flooding an unknown unicast out of all other ports is normal switch behaviour, alongside learning and forwarding/filtering, and the switch learns the correct port when the reply comes back. Dropping the frame is what a router does when no route matches - a switch does not behave that way.

q: Which switch forwarding method reads the entire frame and checks its CRC before forwarding it?

opts.A: Store-and-forward
opts.B: Cut-through
opts.C: Fragment-free
opts.D: Pass-through

exp: Store-and-forward buffers the whole frame and verifies the frame check sequence, so it is the slowest method but never forwards a corrupt frame. Cut-through starts sending as soon as it has read the destination MAC and therefore forwards errors too, while fragment-free reads only the first 64 bytes as a compromise.

q: A router's table holds both 192.168.10.0/24 and 192.168.0.0/16. A packet arrives destined for 192.168.10.5. Which route is used, and why?

opts.A: 192.168.0.0/16, because it was configured first
opts.B: 192.168.0.0/16, because it covers the larger range of addresses
opts.C: 192.168.10.0/24, because it is the longest (most specific) prefix match
opts.D: Neither; the router floods the packet out of all its interfaces

exp: Routing table lookup uses longest prefix match, so the most specific route that covers the destination wins regardless of its position in the table. A router never floods - if nothing matches and there is no default route, it simply drops the packet.

q: Which routing table entry is used when no more specific route matches a packet's destination?
exp: 0.0.0.0/0 is the default route, the least specific entry possible, and in a typical office it points at the ISP link so that all unknown destinations leave through it. 127.0.0.1 is the loopback address and 255.255.255.255 is the limited broadcast address; neither appears as a forwarding destination.

q: What is the essential difference between a gateway and a router?

opts.A: A gateway forwards traffic faster because it does not need to read the IP header
opts.B: A gateway translates between networks using different protocols or data formats, while a router forwards between IP networks that already use the same protocol
opts.C: A gateway works only at Layer 2 while a router works only at Layer 3
opts.D: A gateway can join only two LANs of exactly the same type

exp: A gateway converts - a VoIP gateway between IP telephony and the telephone network, an email gateway between an internal messaging system and SMTP - whereas a router simply forwards IP packets between IP networks. Because translation costs processing, a gateway is typically slower per packet than a router, and it is not confined to any one OSI layer.

q: The 'default gateway' setting on a PC holds which of the following?

opts.A: The IP address of a router interface on the PC's own subnet, to which it sends traffic bound for other networks
opts.B: The address of the DNS server that resolves names outside the organisation
opts.C: A protocol-translating appliance that converts Ethernet frames into IP packets
opts.D: The broadcast address of the PC's local subnet

exp: The default gateway is the next-hop address a host uses for any destination outside its own subnet, and on almost every LAN that address belongs to a router interface. The name is historical - the default gateway is doing routing, not the protocol translation that defines a gateway in the strict sense.

q: Which type of firewall keeps a connection state table, so that return traffic belonging to a session started from inside the network is permitted without a separate rule?

opts.A: A packet-filtering firewall
opts.B: An application-layer (proxy) firewall
opts.C: A stateful inspection firewall
opts.D: A host-based antivirus scanner

exp: Stateful inspection records each connection the inside initiates and derives permission for the reply traffic from that table. A stateless packet filter judges every packet in isolation on the five-tuple and therefore needs an explicit rule for the return direction; an antivirus scanner is not a firewall at all, as it inspects files for malware rather than permitting or blocking traffic.

q: How is a firewall's rule list normally processed?

opts.A: The most specific rule is applied first, wherever it appears in the list
opts.B: From the bottom of the list upwards, and the last match wins
opts.C: Every rule is evaluated and any deny overrides all the allows
opts.D: From the top of the list downwards, the first matching rule wins, and an implicit deny-all ends the list

exp: Rules are evaluated top down and processing stops at the first match, which is why rule order changes behaviour and a broad allow placed above a narrow deny makes the deny useless. Anything reaching the end of the list without matching is dropped by the implicit deny-all.

q: What is the primary function of a wireless access point?

opts.A: To bridge Wi-Fi clients onto an existing wired LAN
opts.B: To route packets between two different IP networks
opts.C: To assign IP addresses to wireless clients from its own pool
opts.D: To translate private internal addresses into a single public address

exp: An access point is a Layer 2 device that puts frames arriving over the radio onto the wired segment and vice versa, extending an existing LAN. Routing, DHCP and NAT belong to the wireless router sold for home use, which is a router plus a switch plus an AP bundled into one box.

q: Two access points in an office building are configured with the same SSID and set to non-overlapping channels. What is the result?

opts.A: Two separate wireless networks, between which a user must manually choose
opts.B: Clients are refused association because the SSID is duplicated
opts.C: A single wireless network across which a user can roam without reconnecting
opts.D: The second AP becomes a repeater and halves the throughput of the first

exp: Sharing one SSID across several cabled APs is exactly how roaming is provided - the client re-associates to whichever AP it hears best while staying on the same network. Halved throughput belongs to a repeater or mesh node relaying an existing signal; an AP with its own Ethernet uplink has no such penalty.

q: Which DNS record type maps a domain name to an IPv4 address?

opts.A: CNAME
opts.B: A
opts.C: MX
opts.D: PTR

exp: An A record holds an IPv4 address for a name, and AAAA does the same job for IPv6. A CNAME is only an alias pointing at another name rather than at an address, MX names the mail server for a domain, and PTR is used for reverse lookups from address back to name.

q: With nothing in its cache, in what order does a recursive resolver query servers to resolve www.mizoram.gov.in?

opts.A: The authoritative server, then the TLD server, then a root server
opts.B: The client's hosts file, then the office router, then the web server itself
opts.C: A TLD server, then a root server, then the authoritative server
opts.D: A root server, then the .in TLD servers, then the authoritative server for the zone

exp: The namespace is hierarchical, so resolution walks down it - root, then the top-level domain, then the delegated zone's own name servers - and the recursive resolver does all that chasing on the client's behalf before returning one final answer. Only the domain's own name servers are authoritative; the resolver a client is configured with is not authoritative for anything.

q: What is the correct order of the four messages exchanged when a client obtains an address from a DHCP server?

opts.A: Discover, Offer, Request, Acknowledge
opts.B: Discover, Request, Offer, Acknowledge
opts.C: Request, Offer, Discover, Acknowledge
opts.D: Offer, Discover, Request, Acknowledge

exp: The sequence is remembered as DORA: the client broadcasts a Discover because it has no address yet, a server replies with an Offer of an available address, the client broadcasts a Request accepting that particular offer, and the server sends an Acknowledge recording the lease. The client cannot Request before an Offer exists, which rules out the other orders.

q: A Windows PC on an office LAN shows the IP address 169.254.14.7. What does this indicate?

opts.A: The DHCP server has issued it an address from its reserved range
opts.B: An administrator has configured a static address on the machine
opts.C: The PC could not reach a DHCP server and has self-assigned an APIPA address
opts.D: The PC received an address but no default gateway from DHCP

exp: 169.254.x.x is the APIPA range a Windows client assigns itself when no DHCP server answers, so it is a symptom of DHCP failure rather than of DHCP working. A reservation still comes out of the server's own scope and would appear as a normal address on the office subnet.

q: Which pair of mechanisms together define a VPN?

opts.A: Compression and caching
opts.B: Tunnelling (encapsulation) and encryption
opts.C: Address translation and port forwarding
opts.D: Load balancing and failover

exp: Tunnelling carries the original packet, private addresses and all, as payload inside an outer packet between the two VPN endpoints, and encryption makes the captured traffic unreadable in transit. Encapsulation on its own gives private addressing but no confidentiality, so it is not a VPN.

q: A district office LAN is permanently joined to the headquarters LAN through VPN devices at each end, and staff on either side reach the other network without installing any software. What kind of VPN is this?

opts.A: A remote-access VPN
opts.B: A client-to-client VPN
opts.C: A split-tunnel remote-access VPN
opts.D: A site-to-site VPN

exp: A site-to-site VPN joins two whole networks through gateway devices, so the tunnel is built between those devices and individual user machines need no client of their own. A remote-access VPN is the opposite case - one user's laptop or phone connecting in through client software.

q: How does PAT (NAT overload) allow many internal hosts to share a single public IP address?

opts.A: It gives each connection a distinct source port number and records the mapping in a translation table
opts.B: It lends the public address to each internal host in turn for a few seconds at a time
opts.C: It compresses the traffic of several hosts into a single packet before sending it
opts.D: It issues each host its own public address from a pool of spare public addresses

exp: PAT rewrites the private source address to the router's public address and assigns each connection a unique source port, so the translation table can steer each reply back to the right internal host. Handing out separate public addresses from a pool is a different mechanism and would defeat the purpose of conserving IPv4 addresses.

q: What is the essential difference between NAT and a proxy server?

opts.A: NAT operates at the application layer while a proxy operates at the network layer
opts.B: Both terminate the client's connection, but NAT additionally caches the content it passes
opts.C: NAT rewrites addresses in packet headers at the network layer and passes the same connection through, while a proxy terminates the client's connection at the application layer and opens its own
opts.D: NAT can filter websites by URL, whereas a proxy cannot

exp: NAT is a header rewrite: the connection itself is never broken and the payload is never examined, which is why NAT cannot cache or filter content. A proxy accepts the client's request as a server, then makes its own separate request outward, and that application-layer position is what lets it cache pages and block particular URLs.

q: In a government office all staff PCs are configured to send their web requests to one server, which fetches the pages on their behalf, blocks certain categories of site and keeps an access log per user. That server is acting as

opts.A: A forward proxy
opts.B: A reverse proxy
opts.C: A NAT router
opts.D: A DNS forwarder

exp: A forward proxy acts on behalf of internal clients going out to the internet, which is what allows content filtering, per-user authentication, logging and caching to be enforced in one place. A reverse proxy is the opposite direction: it sits in front of servers and receives requests coming in.

q: Which statement correctly distinguishes a proxy server from NAT?

opts.A: NAT works at the application layer while a proxy works at the data link layer
opts.B: Both terminate the client's connection, but only NAT is able to cache content
opts.C: A proxy terminates the client's connection and originates its own request at the application layer, while NAT only rewrites addresses and ports in the packet header
opts.D: NAT can filter web content by category, while a proxy can only translate port numbers

exp: A proxy ends the client's connection and makes a fresh request of its own at the application layer, which is exactly why it can read, cache and filter the content it relays. NAT operates at the network layer and merely rewrites header addresses, letting the original connection continue, so it can do neither.

q: Which of the following correctly pairs an 802.11 standard with the frequency band it uses?

opts.A: 802.11a operates in the 2.4 GHz band
opts.B: 802.11a operates in the 5 GHz band
opts.C: 802.11b operates in the 5 GHz band
opts.D: 802.11g operates in the 5 GHz band

exp: 802.11a is the 5 GHz standard, while 802.11b and 802.11g both work in 2.4 GHz, which is why 802.11a equipment is not compatible with b/g equipment. The alphabetical order misleads candidates into assuming 'a' came first and must therefore be the 2.4 GHz one.

q: Which Wi-Fi standard was the first to operate in both the 2.4 GHz and 5 GHz bands and introduced MIMO with multiple antennas?
exp: 802.11n, marketed as Wi-Fi 4, was the first amendment to work on both bands and the first to use MIMO for parallel data streams. 802.11ac (Wi-Fi 5) is a later standard but operates in the 5 GHz band only, so dual-band operation did not begin with it.

q: Which sequence lists Wi-Fi security standards from the oldest and weakest to the newest and strongest?

opts.A: WEP, WPA, WPA2, WPA3
opts.B: WPA, WEP, WPA2, WPA3
opts.C: WEP, WPA2, WPA, WPA3
opts.D: WPA2, WPA, WEP, WPA3

exp: The succession is WEP, then WPA, then WPA2, then WPA3, each correcting weaknesses in the one before. WEP is comprehensively broken and must never be configured, WPA was an interim fix using TKIP, WPA2 introduced AES-CCMP, and WPA3 replaces the pre-shared key handshake with SAE.

q: What does WPA2-Enterprise provide that WPA2-Personal does not?

opts.A: AES encryption in place of TKIP
opts.B: Automatic hiding of the SSID from scanning devices
opts.C: Per-user authentication using 802.1X and a RADIUS server instead of one shared passphrase
opts.D: MAC address filtering enforced at the access point

exp: Enterprise mode authenticates every user separately through 802.1X against a RADIUS server, typically backed by Active Directory, so one employee's wireless access can be revoked by a single account change. AES-CCMP is not the difference: both Personal and Enterprise modes of WPA2 use it, and Personal simply shares one passphrase among all users.

q: GSM belongs to which generation of mobile networks?

opts.A: 3G
opts.B: 1G
opts.C: 4G
opts.D: 2G

exp: GSM is the dominant 2G family, the first digital generation, and it brought SIM cards, SMS and usable call encryption. It is regularly mis-offered as 3G, but 3G means UMTS/WCDMA and CDMA2000; GPRS and EDGE are data add-ons to 2G, not a separate generation.

q: What is the key architectural change introduced by 4G LTE?

opts.A: It introduced SIM cards and SMS messaging for the first time
opts.B: It was the first generation to use digital radio instead of analogue
opts.C: It moved the network to all-IP, with voice carried over the data network as VoLTE
opts.D: It introduced network slicing and millimetre-wave spectrum

exp: 4G LTE is an all-IP network with no separate circuit-switched voice path, so calls run over the data network as VoLTE. Network slicing and millimetre wave are the defining additions of 5G, not 4G, and SIM cards and digital radio arrived with 2G.

q: In Windows Server, major services such as Active Directory Domain Services, DNS and Hyper-V are installed as

opts.A: Roles
opts.B: Features
opts.C: Snap-ins
opts.D: Editions

exp: A role is the main service a server provides and is added through Server Manager or PowerShell. A feature is a supporting component such as failover clustering or Windows Server Backup, so calling Hyper-V or AD DS a feature is the standard error.

q: Which statement about a Windows workgroup is correct?

opts.A: All member computers share one account database held on a domain controller
opts.B: Each computer keeps its own local accounts, so a user needs an account on every machine
opts.C: Group Policy is applied centrally to every workgroup member at logon
opts.D: A workgroup requires Active Directory and DNS service records to function

exp: In a workgroup every computer holds its own local account database, so there is no central authentication and no central policy; that is workable for a handful of PCs and unmanageable for fifty. A central account store, Group Policy and dependence on DNS service records all belong to a domain, which is why a government office network is always a domain.

q: What is the correct order in which Group Policy Objects are processed?

opts.A: Site, Local, Domain, Organisational Unit
opts.B: Domain, Site, Organisational Unit, Local
opts.C: Local, Site, Domain, Organisational Unit
opts.D: Organisational Unit, Domain, Site, Local

exp: The order is Local, Site, Domain, Organisational Unit, remembered as LSDOU, and later processing overwrites earlier on a conflict, so the OU-level GPO normally wins. Candidates commonly reverse it and assume local policy is applied last, when in fact it is applied first and is overridden by everything above it.

q: An administrator wants a password and account-lockout policy to apply to a set of machines regardless of which user logs on. In which half of the Group Policy Object should the setting be placed, and when is it applied?

opts.A: User Configuration, applied at logon
opts.B: User Configuration, applied at startup
opts.C: Computer Configuration, applied at logon
opts.D: Computer Configuration, applied at startup

exp: Computer Configuration applies to the machine whoever signs in to it and is processed at startup; User Configuration applies to the account wherever it signs in and is processed at logon. A setting placed in the wrong half does not raise an error, it simply never takes effect.

q: What is the recommended way to give an entire department access to a shared folder in an Active Directory domain?

opts.A: Grant the permission to each user account individually
opts.B: Grant the permission to a distribution group containing those users
opts.C: Grant the permission to the organisational unit that contains those users
opts.D: Grant the permission to a security group and add the users to that group

exp: Permissions are assigned to security groups, and access is then granted or removed simply by changing group membership, which stays auditable a year later. A distribution group is a mailing list and can hold no permissions at all, and an organisational unit is a container for applying Group Policy and delegating administration, not something you grant folder rights to.

q: An account that exists only in the SAM database of one computer and cannot be used to log on to any other machine is

opts.A: A domain account
opts.B: A local account
opts.C: A universal group
opts.D: A global catalog account

exp: A local account lives in the SAM database of a single computer and works only there, which is why it suits a standalone machine or an emergency administrator login. A domain account lives in Active Directory and works on every domain-joined machine, with one password and one place to disable it when a staff member leaves.

q: A user reaches a shared folder across the network. The share permission is Full Control and the NTFS permission on the folder is Read. What is the user's effective permission?

opts.A: Full Control
opts.B: Change
opts.C: Read
opts.D: No access

exp: When both sets are evaluated for network access, the more restrictive result wins, so Full Control on the share combined with Read on NTFS gives Read. Candidates often add the two together or take the more generous one; the rule is the opposite.

q: Which statement about share permissions and NTFS permissions is correct?

opts.A: Share permissions apply only to access arriving over the network, while NTFS permissions apply both locally and over the network
opts.B: NTFS permissions apply only over the network, while share permissions also apply to a user sitting at the machine
opts.C: Both share and NTFS permissions apply only to access over the network
opts.D: Share permissions can be set separately on each file and subfolder inside the share

exp: Share permissions govern network access only and are set on the share as a whole, offering just Read, Change and Full Control. NTFS permissions are stored on the file system, are far finer grained, and restrict a user whether they come across the network or log on at the console, which is why only NTFS can control local access.

q: Remote Desktop Protocol listens on which TCP port by default?
exp: RDP uses TCP port 3389. Port 443 is associated with RDS only indirectly, because an RD Gateway tunnels RDP inside HTTPS so that 3389 need never be exposed to the internet.

q: Which Remote Desktop Services capability publishes a single application so that it appears in its own window on the user's own desktop, instead of presenting a whole remote desktop?

opts.A: RemoteApp
opts.B: RD Gateway
opts.C: Connection Broker
opts.D: RD Licensing

exp: RemoteApp publishes an individual program that runs on the session host but appears in a normal window alongside the user's local applications. RD Gateway tunnels RDP inside HTTPS for external users, the Connection Broker directs users to the right session host and reconnects existing sessions, and RD Licensing issues the client access licences.

q: Under the shared responsibility model, who patches the guest operating system of a virtual machine running in an IaaS cloud?

opts.A: The cloud provider, as part of maintaining the hypervisor
opts.B: The customer, who owns the operating system and the application on it
opts.C: The hardware vendor who supplied the provider's servers
opts.D: Nobody, because IaaS virtual machines do not require operating system patches

exp: In IaaS the provider maintains the facility, hardware and hypervisor, while the customer installs and patches the operating system and application. Only from PaaS upwards does the provider take over OS and platform patching, and in every model the customer still remains responsible for his own data and user access.

q: A department keeps sensitive records on a private cloud dedicated to itself, runs its public website on a shared public cloud, and connects the two so workloads can move between them. This arrangement is called

opts.A: Public cloud
opts.B: Private cloud
opts.C: Community cloud
opts.D: Hybrid cloud

exp: A hybrid cloud joins public and private cloud so that workloads can move between them. A community cloud is different: it is shared by several organisations with a common requirement, such as a group of government departments, rather than combining two deployment models used by one organisation.

q: Two computers are plugged into the same physical switch but have been placed in different VLANs. What is required for them to communicate with each other?

opts.A: Nothing, because they are on the same switch they communicate directly at layer 2
opts.B: A router or a layer 3 switch to route between the two VLANs
opts.C: A repeater installed between the two switch ports
opts.D: A trunk port configured on the switch

exp: A VLAN is layer 2 segmentation, so ports in different VLANs are in separate broadcast domains and cannot reach each other even on the same switch; traffic between them must pass through a router or layer 3 switch. A trunk port is not the answer: it carries several tagged VLANs between switches but performs no routing.

q: In a cloud virtual network, what is a security group?

opts.A: A stateful set of rules acting as a virtual firewall on a subnet or a network interface
opts.B: A group of user accounts permitted to create virtual machines
opts.C: A set of virtual machines that share a single public IP address
opts.D: A physical firewall appliance installed in the provider's data centre

exp: A cloud security group is a stateful rule list attached to a subnet or a virtual machine's network interface, permitting or denying traffic by source, destination, protocol and port. It is not the same thing as an Active Directory security group of user accounts, and it does not replace a firewall appliance since it performs no deep inspection or content filtering.

q: In Microsoft Azure, a resource group is best described as

opts.A: A geographic area containing one or more Azure data centres
opts.B: The billing boundary against which all usage charges accumulate
opts.C: A logical container holding related resources, to which permissions can be applied and whose deletion removes everything inside it
opts.D: A physically separate data centre with independent power, cooling and networking

exp: A resource group is a management container that groups the resources of one application or department; access permissions are applied at group level and deleting the group deletes its contents. The billing boundary is the subscription, not the resource group, and every resource belongs to exactly one resource group.

q: Deploying an application across two availability zones inside the same Azure region mainly protects the application against

opts.A: Failure of a single data centre, since zones have independent power, cooling and networking
opts.B: Loss of the entire region in which the application is deployed
opts.C: Accidental deletion of the resource group containing the application
opts.D: Exceeding the service limits and quotas that apply to the subscription

exp: Availability zones are physically separate data centres within one region, each with its own power, cooling and networking, so spreading across zones keeps the application running when one data centre fails. Surviving the loss of a whole region is a different scale of problem and requires deployment into a second region.

q: In SNMP-based network monitoring, an SNMP trap is

opts.A: A request sent by the monitoring station to read a counter from a device
opts.B: A text event message written to a central syslog server
opts.C: A threshold value configured on the monitoring station
opts.D: An unsolicited message pushed by the device's agent to the manager when an event occurs

exp: A trap travels from the agent on the device to the manager the moment an event happens, so a link failure is reported immediately instead of waiting for the next poll. Polling is the opposite direction — the manager queries the agent's MIB counters on a schedule.

q: Recording a network's normal traffic and performance values over a representative period, so that alert thresholds can later be set relative to normal behaviour, is called

opts.A: Polling
opts.B: Baselining
opts.C: Trapping
opts.D: Log rotation

exp: Baselining establishes what normal looks like, which is what makes an abnormal reading recognisable — without it, high utilisation cannot be distinguished from a merely busy period. Polling is the act of querying devices for counters and is how the baseline data is collected, not the recording of normal behaviour itself.

q: A user cannot reach a remote server, and the administrator wants to see each router along the way and identify the point at which traffic stops. Which command is most appropriate?

opts.A: ping
opts.B: netstat
opts.C: tracert
opts.D: ipconfig

exp: Tracert on Windows (traceroute on Linux) lists every router hop on the path to the destination, so the hop at which replies stop isolates the faulty link or router. Ping only reports end-to-end reachability and round-trip time; it says nothing about where along the path the failure occurs.

q: A workstation successfully pings a web server by its IP address but fails when the server's name is used. Which command should the administrator use next to check name resolution specifically?

opts.A: nslookup
opts.B: netstat
opts.C: traceroute
opts.D: ifconfig

exp: Nslookup queries DNS and shows whether the name resolves and which server answered, which is exactly the fault indicated when the IP address works but the name does not. Netstat lists active connections, listening ports and the routing table, and would not reveal a DNS failure.

q: Which group of SQL commands makes up the Transaction Control Language (TCL)?

opts.A: CREATE, ALTER, DROP
opts.B: COMMIT, ROLLBACK, SAVEPOINT
opts.C: GRANT, REVOKE
opts.D: SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE

exp: TCL manages transactions, and its commands are COMMIT (make the changes permanent), ROLLBACK (undo them) and SAVEPOINT (mark a point for a partial rollback). GRANT and REVOKE are the tempting wrong pick: they are DCL, the Data Control Language used for privileges, not for transactions.

q: A transaction deletes rows from a table and then issues ROLLBACK. Which statement about DELETE and TRUNCATE is correct?

opts.A: Both DELETE and TRUNCATE can always be reversed by ROLLBACK
opts.B: Neither DELETE nor TRUNCATE can ever be reversed by ROLLBACK
opts.C: A DELETE can be rolled back, but TRUNCATE is DDL and carries an implicit commit, so it normally cannot
opts.D: A TRUNCATE can be rolled back, but a DELETE writes directly to disk and cannot

exp: DELETE is a DML statement and its work stays inside the open transaction until COMMIT, so ROLLBACK undoes it. TRUNCATE is DDL, and a DDL statement issues an implicit commit that closes the transaction, which is why the rows are normally gone for good.

q: In a relational database, a view is best described as

opts.A: a virtual table defined by a stored SELECT query, which holds no data of its own
opts.B: a physical copy of selected rows kept in a separate table
opts.C: a temporary table that stores rows for the duration of the session
opts.D: an index structure that speeds up retrieval from a large table

exp: Only the query definition is stored, in the data dictionary; the rows are produced by running that query against the base tables each time the view is used. A temporary table is the tempting distractor, but it really holds rows for the session, whereas a view holds none at any time.

q: A clerk must be able to read employee names and departments but not the salary column. What is the standard way to arrange this using a view?

opts.A: Encrypt the salary column and give the clerk SELECT on the base table
opts.B: Create an index on name and department and grant it to the clerk
opts.C: Delete the salary column from the table whenever the clerk logs in
opts.D: Create a view selecting only name and department, and grant SELECT on the view instead of on the base table

exp: Granting privileges on a view rather than on the base table is a standard access-control mechanism: the view exposes only the chosen columns (or, with a WHERE clause, only the chosen rows) and the clerk never touches the base table. An index is a performance structure and grants no access at all.

q: What is the main disadvantage of creating an index on many columns of a heavily updated table?

opts.A: Queries return incorrect results because the index changes the row order
opts.B: The table can no longer be joined to other tables
opts.C: Every INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE must also maintain each index, so writes slow down and extra storage is used
opts.D: The primary key constraint is dropped automatically

exp: An index has to be kept in step with the table, so each additional index adds work to every write and occupies extra disk space. "More indexes always make the database faster" is the classic wrong answer; an index never alters the result of a query, only the time taken to get it.

q: Why can a table have only one clustered index?

opts.A: Because a clustered index determines the physical order in which the table's rows are stored
opts.B: Because a clustered index can be built on only one column
opts.C: Because the DBMS reserves the remaining index slots for foreign keys
opts.D: Because a clustered index stores a copy of the whole table and space allows only one copy

exp: A clustered index fixes the physical sequence of the rows themselves, and rows can be laid out in only one order at a time. A non-clustered index is a separate structure of key values and row pointers, so a table may carry many of those.

q: What is the key difference between a stored procedure and a trigger?

opts.A: A stored procedure is written in SQL while a trigger is written in the application's programming language
opts.B: A stored procedure must be called explicitly, whereas a trigger fires automatically when a data event occurs on a table
opts.C: A stored procedure runs on the client machine while a trigger runs on the server
opts.D: A stored procedure can read data only, whereas a trigger can also modify data

exp: A procedure is invoked by name with CALL or EXECUTE and does nothing until something asks for it; a trigger is attached to a table and is set off by an INSERT, UPDATE or DELETE without the application asking. Both live and run on the database server, so the client-versus-server option is wrong.

q: Which of the following is a genuine security advantage of using stored procedures?

opts.A: They encrypt the data in the tables they read
opts.B: They remove the need for users to authenticate to the database
opts.C: They automatically create an audit trail of every statement executed
opts.D: A user can be granted EXECUTE on the procedure without being granted any privilege on the underlying tables

exp: Granting EXECUTE lets a user touch the data only in the controlled ways the procedure allows, while the tables themselves stay closed to them, and passing values as parameters also resists SQL injection. Procedures neither encrypt data nor log activity by themselves; that is the work of encryption and auditing.

q: Transaction T2 reads a value that T1 has changed but not yet committed, and T1 then rolls back. What is this concurrency problem called?

opts.A: Dirty read
opts.B: Lost update
opts.C: Non-repeatable read
opts.D: Phantom read

exp: Reading uncommitted data that is later rolled back is a dirty read, also called an uncommitted dependency, because T2 has acted on a value that never really existed. A non-repeatable read is different: there the second transaction did commit, and the problem is that a re-read of the same row now returns a different value.

q: Under the two-phase locking protocol, a transaction

opts.A: acquires all its locks at the very start and releases them one at a time as it works
opts.B: must write its changes to two separate disks before committing
opts.C: has a growing phase in which it only acquires locks and a shrinking phase in which it only releases them
opts.D: coordinates its COMMIT across two or more databases before the change becomes permanent

exp: Two-phase locking divides a transaction into a growing phase, where locks may only be taken, and a shrinking phase, where they may only be released; once any lock has been released no further lock may be acquired, and this guarantees a serialisable schedule. Option D describes two-phase commit, a distributed-transaction protocol with a confusingly similar name.

q: In database security, what is the difference between authentication and authorization?

opts.A: Authentication decides what a user may do; authorization checks the user's password
opts.B: Authentication verifies who is connecting; authorization decides what that identity is then permitted to do
opts.C: Authentication applies to administrators only; authorization applies to ordinary users
opts.D: Authentication converts stored data into ciphertext; authorization decrypts it for approved users

exp: Authentication answers "who are you?" and always comes first; authorization, enforced through GRANT and REVOKE, then answers "what may you do?". A user can be perfectly authenticated and still be authorized for nothing at all.

q: A government office runs a Windows domain and configures its database to accept Windows / Active Directory accounts instead of passwords stored in the database. What is the main advantage of this integrated authentication?

opts.A: The data files on disk become encrypted automatically
opts.B: Users no longer need any privileges granted to them on the tables
opts.C: The database can then be installed without a database administrator
opts.D: Password policy, expiry and de-provisioning when staff leave are handled centrally in the directory, and users get single sign-on

exp: Delegating identity checking to the operating system or directory service means password strength, expiry, lockout and account removal are managed once for the whole organisation, and the user connects without retyping a password. Authorization is unaffected: those directory identities still have to be mapped to logins and granted privileges.

q: Transparent Data Encryption (TDE) in a database protects against which situation?

opts.A: Someone who steals the disk or a backup copy of the database files
opts.B: A legitimately logged-in user querying a table they should not see
opts.C: An attacker capturing the client-to-server network traffic
opts.D: A database administrator deleting rows from a sensitive table

exp: TDE encrypts the whole datafile and its backups at the storage layer, so a stolen disk or backup tape is unreadable, but the engine decrypts pages transparently for anyone who logs in legitimately. Hiding a value from an authorised or privileged user querying the table requires column-level encryption instead, and network traffic needs TLS.

q: Which practice is essential for database encryption to be of any real value?

opts.A: Storing the encryption key in a table inside the same database it protects
opts.B: Keeping the key in a configuration file on the database server for fast access
opts.C: Keeping the key in a separate keystore, HSM or key-management service, with its own protected backup
opts.D: Changing the encryption algorithm every time a backup is taken

exp: Ciphertext is only as safe as its key, so an attacker who takes the server must not take both halves; keys belong in a separate protected store with rotation and their own backup, because losing the key makes the data permanently unrecoverable. Storing the key beside the data, in the database or in a file on the same machine, defeats the whole exercise.

q: Database auditing is best described as which kind of security control?

opts.A: A preventive control that blocks unauthorised statements before they run
opts.B: A detective control that records activity so misuse can be attributed afterwards
opts.C: A recovery control that restores rows deleted by mistake
opts.D: A corrective control that automatically revokes a user's privileges on misuse

exp: An audit trail records who did what, to which object, and when — including failed attempts — so that every action is attributable to a named account, but it stops nothing by itself. Preventing an unauthorised action is authorization's job, and restoring lost rows is backup and recovery's.

q: How does a database audit trail differ from the transaction log?

opts.A: They are two names for the same file
opts.B: The audit trail is used by the engine for rollback, while the transaction log is read by investigators
opts.C: The audit trail records only failed statements, while the transaction log records only successful ones
opts.D: The transaction log exists so the engine can roll back and recover, while the audit trail exists so a human can hold someone accountable

exp: The transaction log is consumed by the recovery manager to redo committed and undo uncommitted work; the audit trail is read by people to establish accountability and support forensic investigation. Option B states the correct facts with the two names swapped, which is exactly the trap. Neither file substitutes for the other.

q: Which statement about Microsoft SQL Server is correct?

opts.A: It is a proprietary relational DBMS whose procedural SQL dialect is T-SQL
opts.B: It is an open-source relational DBMS released under a community licence
opts.C: It is a NoSQL document store and does not use SQL
opts.D: It is the only database product in which the SQL language can be used

exp: SQL Server is Microsoft's commercially licensed relational product, and Transact-SQL is its dialect for stored procedures, triggers and functions. The name misleads: SQL is a language every RDBMS uses, so calling the product "SQL Server" does not make it the only one that speaks SQL.

q: Which tool is the standard graphical client for administering and querying Microsoft SQL Server?

opts.A: pgAdmin
opts.B: psql
opts.C: SQL Server Management Studio (SSMS)
opts.D: Microsoft Access

exp: SSMS is Microsoft's graphical administration and query environment for SQL Server. pgAdmin and psql belong to PostgreSQL, and MS Access is a separate desktop database product, not the management console for a SQL Server instance.

q: PostgreSQL is best described as

opts.A: a proprietary database sold by a single vendor under a per-core licence
opts.B: a free and open-source object-relational DBMS maintained by a worldwide community
opts.C: a non-relational key-value store used mainly for caching
opts.D: a spreadsheet-based desktop database for single users

exp: PostgreSQL is community-governed and released under a permissive open-source licence, and it is called object-relational because it adds user-defined types, table inheritance, arrays and JSON on top of ordinary relational tables. Open source means no licence fee and no vendor lock-in, not that running it costs nothing at all.

q: PostgreSQL can store and query JSON documents inside a column. What does this mean?

opts.A: PostgreSQL has become a NoSQL database and no longer supports transactions
opts.B: JSON columns in PostgreSQL cannot be queried, only stored as plain text
opts.C: PostgreSQL must be run alongside MongoDB to use JSON data
opts.D: PostgreSQL remains relational and ACID-compliant; JSON is simply one of its column types

exp: Storing semi-structured documents is one of PostgreSQL's object-relational extras, and the engine still enforces the relational model and full ACID transactions. Relational products supporting JSON is exactly why the SQL/NoSQL line has blurred, but it does not reclassify PostgreSQL as a NoSQL store.

q: Which type of NoSQL database is the natural choice for storing a social network and quickly traversing the connections between people?

opts.A: Graph database
opts.B: Key-value store
opts.C: Column-family (wide-column) store
opts.D: Document store

exp: A graph database treats nodes and the relationships between them as first-class objects, so following connections is direct rather than a chain of joins — Neo4j is the standard example, and fraud-ring detection and recommendation are the same shape of problem. A key-value store fetches a value by its key alone and has no notion of relationships between entries.

q: Relational databases are described as ACID and many NoSQL systems as BASE. What does the BASE trade-off mean in practice?

opts.A: The database performs no validation of the data written to it
opts.B: Transactions are committed twice, once on each of two servers
opts.C: A read taken immediately after a write may return the old value, with the copies converging shortly afterwards
opts.D: The database can never lose data, even if every server fails at once

exp: BASE stands for Basically Available, Soft state, Eventual consistency, so consistency is reached after a short delay rather than guaranteed at the instant of the read. A relational ACID system guarantees you read exactly what you just wrote, which is why money, ledgers and other integrity-critical data still belong there.

q: When a user types www.mizoram.gov.in into a web browser, what is the main job of the Domain Name System?

opts.A: To encrypt the data sent between the browser and the website
opts.B: To translate the typed domain name into the IP address of the server hosting the site
opts.C: To compress the web pages so that they download faster
opts.D: To check that the content of the website is safe to view

exp: DNS is the naming service that maps human-readable domain names to the numeric IP addresses that computers actually use to connect, so the browser can reach the correct server. Encryption of the connection is done by HTTPS/TLS, which is a separate mechanism from name resolution.

q: In the web address www.mizoram.gov.in, which part is the top-level domain (TLD)?

opts.A: www
opts.B: mizoram
opts.C: gov
opts.D: in

exp: Domain names are read from right to left, so the last label, in, is the top-level domain, in this case India's country-code TLD. Under it, gov.in is the second-level domain reserved for government bodies, while www is only a host label at the front of the name.

q: What is the Document Object Model (DOM) of a web page?

opts.A: A file format used to store web pages on the server's hard disk
opts.B: A style sheet language used to control the layout of a page
opts.C: A tree-structured representation of the page's elements that a script can read and change
opts.D: A protocol used to transfer web pages from the server to the browser

exp: When a browser loads a page it builds the DOM, a tree of objects in which each element, attribute and piece of text is a node that JavaScript can inspect, modify, add or remove, with the display updating immediately. Controlling layout and appearance is the job of CSS, which is a separate language from the DOM.

q: In JavaScript, what is an event listener attached to a DOM element used for?

opts.A: To run a piece of code whenever a specified action, such as a click, happens on that element
opts.B: To load an external style sheet into the page
opts.C: To check the page's HTML for spelling and syntax errors before it is displayed
opts.D: To measure how long the page takes to download from the server

exp: An event listener registers a function that the browser calls when a named event, such as a click, key press or form submission, occurs on the element, which is how a page responds to the user without reloading. Downloading and rendering the page itself happens before any listener fires and is not what a listener controls.

q: In a REST API, which HTTP method is normally used to fetch a resource without changing it?

opts.A: POST
opts.B: GET
opts.C: PUT
opts.D: DELETE

exp: GET simply requests a copy of the resource identified by the URL and is meant to be safe, that is, repeating it leaves the data on the server unchanged. POST is used to send new data to the server and may create a record each time it is repeated, so it is not a read-only method.

q: A REST API is described as 'stateless'. What does this mean?

opts.A: The API can return only data that never changes
opts.B: The server stores each client's session details between requests
opts.C: Each request carries all the information needed to process it, and the server keeps no memory of the client's earlier requests
opts.D: The API works only when the client and the server are on the same local network

exp: Statelessness means every request is self-contained, carrying its own identification and parameters, so any server in a pool can handle it and nothing about the previous request needs to be remembered. Keeping a per-client session on the server is exactly the stateful behaviour that REST avoids.

q: What does the abbreviation JSON stand for?

opts.A: JavaScript Object Notation
opts.B: Java Standard Object Naming
opts.C: JavaScript Online Network
opts.D: Joined Structured Object Notation

exp: JSON stands for JavaScript Object Notation, a lightweight text format for exchanging data, most commonly between a web page and a server. It has nothing to do with the Java language, which is a different language from JavaScript.

q: Although its name mentions JavaScript, which of the following statements about JSON is correct?

opts.A: JSON data can be opened only inside a web browser
opts.B: JSON data can be produced and read only by programs written in JavaScript
opts.C: JSON is a compiled binary format and cannot be read as ordinary text
opts.D: JSON is a plain-text data format that programs written in almost any language can produce and read

exp: JSON only borrowed its notation from JavaScript; it is a language-independent text format, and Python, Java, C#, PHP and most other languages have built-in support for reading and writing it. Because it is plain text made up of objects, arrays, strings, numbers, true, false and null, it can also be opened in any ordinary text editor.

q: Which of the following best describes a Progressive Web Application (PWA)?

opts.A: A website whose images gradually load from top to bottom as the user scrolls
opts.B: A web application built with standard web technologies that can be installed on a device's home screen and behave much like a native app
opts.C: A desktop program written in C++ whose only purpose is to display web pages
opts.D: A server-side program that generates HTML pages on demand from a database

exp: A PWA is an ordinary web app, delivered over the web and built with HTML, CSS and JavaScript, that additionally can be added to the home screen, run in its own window, work offline and show notifications, so it bridges the gap between web and native apps. Generating HTML on the server describes a conventional dynamic website, which is not what makes an app 'progressive'.

q: Which component of a Progressive Web Application makes it possible for the app to keep working when the device has no internet connection?

opts.A: The site's CSS style sheet
opts.B: The DNS resolver on the device
opts.C: The service worker, a background script that can store and serve cached files
opts.D: The web server's access log

exp: A service worker is a script the browser runs in the background, separate from the page, which can intercept network requests and answer them from a local cache, allowing the app to open and function offline. A style sheet only controls appearance and cannot supply the app's data or pages.

q: The Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG) are organised around four principles. Which set names them correctly?

opts.A: Perceivable, Operable, Understandable, Robust
opts.B: Portable, Optimised, Uniform, Responsive
opts.C: Public, Open, Usable, Reliable
opts.D: Perceivable, Ordered, Universal, Readable

exp: WCAG groups its requirements under Perceivable, Operable, Understandable and Robust, often remembered as POUR, covering things such as text alternatives for images, full keyboard operation, clear language and adequate colour contrast. The other lists mix in performance and design terms that are not accessibility principles.

q: Which Indian law requires that information and communication services, including government websites, be made accessible to persons with disabilities?

opts.A: The Information Technology Act, 2000
opts.B: The Rights of Persons with Disabilities Act, 2016
opts.C: The Right to Information Act, 2005
opts.D: The Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023

exp: The Rights of Persons with Disabilities Act, 2016 obliges the government to ensure that information and communication technology, including websites and electronic services, is accessible, and the Guidelines for Indian Government Websites (GIGW) set out how departments should meet this in practice. The Information Technology Act deals with electronic records, digital signatures and cyber offences, not accessibility.

q: A padlock icon shown beside a website's address in the browser indicates that

opts.A: the website has been inspected and approved by the government
opts.B: the website cannot be attacked by hackers
opts.C: the connection between the browser and the website is encrypted using HTTPS
opts.D: the website does not store any cookies on the user's computer

exp: The padlock only means the traffic is protected by TLS, so data such as passwords cannot be read or altered in transit by anyone intercepting the connection. It says nothing about whether the site itself is honest, and fraudulent sites can and do obtain valid certificates, so a padlock is not a guarantee of trustworthiness.

q: Which description best fits an SQL injection attack on a website?

opts.A: Flooding the web server with so many requests that it stops responding to genuine users
opts.B: Automatically trying large numbers of password combinations until one works
opts.C: Intercepting and reading data while it travels between the browser and the server
opts.D: Entering specially crafted text in an input field so that it is treated as part of a database command

exp: In SQL injection the attacker supplies input that the application pastes straight into a database query, so the input is executed as instructions and can reveal or destroy data; the defence is to validate input and use parameterised queries on the server, never relying on browser-side checks alone. Overwhelming a server with traffic is a denial-of-service attack, which is a different category of threat.

q: Which principle of the CIA triad is violated when an attacker alters the amounts stored in a government payroll file?

opts.A: Confidentiality
opts.B: Availability
opts.C: Integrity
opts.D: Non-repudiation

exp: Integrity means data must remain accurate and unaltered except by authorised change, so tampering with stored figures is an integrity breach. Confidentiality would be the answer only if the attacker had merely read or disclosed the data without changing it.

q: Giving a data-entry operator only the access rights needed to do the job, and nothing more, follows which security principle?

opts.A: Principle of least privilege
opts.B: Defence in depth
opts.C: Separation of duties
opts.D: Security through obscurity

exp: Least privilege restricts every user, process or account to the minimum permissions required for its task, limiting the damage if that account is misused. Separation of duties is different: it splits one sensitive task between two people so no single person can complete it alone.

q: Which security service ensures that the sender of a digitally signed message cannot later deny having sent it?

opts.A: Confidentiality
opts.B: Availability
opts.C: Access control
opts.D: Non-repudiation

exp: Non-repudiation provides proof of origin that the sender cannot credibly disown, which is why digital signatures are given legal recognition under the IT Act. Access control decides who may reach a resource, but it says nothing about proving after the fact who performed an action.

q: Malware that encrypts a victim's files and demands payment in exchange for the decryption key is called

opts.A: Spyware
opts.B: Ransomware
opts.C: Adware
opts.D: Rootkit

exp: Ransomware's defining behaviour is encrypting or locking the victim's data and extorting a payment to release it. Spyware also runs secretly, but its purpose is to collect and transmit information rather than to deny the owner access to it.

q: A program that appears to be a useful utility but secretly carries malicious code inside it is best described as a

opts.A: Worm
opts.B: Logic bomb
opts.C: Trojan horse
opts.D: Boot sector virus

exp: A Trojan horse is defined by disguise: the user is tricked into installing it because it looks legitimate. A worm needs no such disguise and no user action at all, since it spreads by itself across a network.

q: An email that appears to come from the user's bank and asks him to click a link and enter his net-banking password is an example of

opts.A: Phishing
opts.B: Denial-of-service attack
opts.C: SQL injection
opts.D: Session hijacking

exp: Phishing uses a forged but convincing message to persuade the victim to hand over credentials or open a malicious link. A denial-of-service attack is aimed at making a service unavailable, not at deceiving a user into revealing a password.

q: The primary function of a firewall in a network is to

opts.A: scan stored files against a database of virus signatures
opts.B: control traffic passing between networks according to a set of rules
opts.C: encrypt every packet that leaves the organisation
opts.D: take periodic backups of server data to a remote site

exp: A firewall sits at a network boundary and permits or blocks traffic by comparing it with a configured rule set (addresses, ports, protocols, connection state). Encryption of traffic is the job of protocols such as TLS or a VPN, which is a separate function from filtering.

q: What distinguishes a stateful inspection firewall from a simple packet-filtering firewall?

opts.A: It filters traffic using only the source IP address of each packet
opts.B: It keeps a permanent copy of every packet it forwards
opts.C: It operates without any configured rule set
opts.D: It tracks active connections and judges each packet in the context of its session

exp: Stateful inspection maintains a connection table, so a reply packet is allowed only if it belongs to a session the firewall has already seen being established. A plain packet filter has no such memory and decides on each packet's header fields in isolation.

q: A firewall configured to block all traffic except that which is explicitly permitted is following a

opts.A: default-deny policy
opts.B: default-allow policy
opts.C: transparent bridging policy
opts.D: port mirroring policy

exp: Default-deny (implicit deny) means anything not matched by an allow rule is dropped, which is the recommended secure baseline. A default-allow policy is the opposite and leaves any service the administrator forgot to block exposed.

q: Signature-based antivirus detection works by

opts.A: comparing the size of every file with a stored backup copy
opts.B: preventing all executable files from running on the machine
opts.C: matching files against a database of known malware patterns
opts.D: encrypting suspicious files so that they cannot execute

exp: A signature is a pattern extracted from known malware, so detection depends on the local signature database being kept up to date. This is also its weakness: a sample the vendor has not yet catalogued will not match any signature.

q: Which antivirus capability is most likely to detect a brand-new (zero-day) malware sample for which no signature has been released?

opts.A: On-demand scanning using the existing signature database
opts.B: Behaviour-based (heuristic) analysis
opts.C: The quarantine folder
opts.D: A scheduled weekly full-disk scan

exp: Heuristic and behavioural engines flag suspicious actions such as mass file encryption or injection into system processes, so they can catch malware that has no signature yet. Quarantine is only where a file is isolated after it has already been detected.

q: In endpoint protection, the abbreviation EDR stands for

opts.A: Encrypted Data Recovery
opts.B: Enterprise Device Registry
opts.C: Endpoint Data Replication
opts.D: Endpoint Detection and Response

exp: EDR is Endpoint Detection and Response: it continuously records endpoint activity so an administrator can detect, investigate and respond to an intrusion, going beyond the block-or-clean model of classic antivirus. The other expansions are not standard security terms.

q: Which of the following login methods is a genuine example of two-factor authentication?

opts.A: A password plus a one-time password sent to the user's registered mobile number
opts.B: A password plus an answer to a security question
opts.C: A password plus a numeric PIN
opts.D: A long password that the user changes every month
