exp: Two-factor authentication needs evidence from two different categories, and a password (something you know) with an OTP on a registered phone (something you have) qualifies. A password with a PIN or a security answer is still two pieces of remembered knowledge, so it remains single-factor.

q: A fingerprint scan used at login belongs to which category of authentication factor?

opts.A: Something you know
opts.B: Something you have
opts.C: Something you are
opts.D: Something you configure

exp: Biometrics such as fingerprint, iris or face are inherence factors: something you are. A smart card or an OTP token would be a possession factor, something you have.

q: Why is multi-factor authentication recommended for government email and eOffice accounts?

opts.A: It removes the need for antivirus software on the user's computer
opts.B: An attacker who steals the password still cannot log in without the second factor
opts.C: It allows the same password to be safely reused on many systems
opts.D: It encrypts all mail already stored on the server

exp: MFA's value is that a leaked, guessed or phished password is no longer sufficient by itself, because the attacker also lacks the registered device or biometric. It does not encrypt stored data and does not make password reuse safe, since a reused password still exposes every other account.

q: In symmetric key encryption,

opts.A: the sender and receiver each use a mathematically related key pair
opts.B: the encryption key is published openly in a directory
opts.C: no key is needed at the receiver's end
opts.D: the same secret key is used both to encrypt and to decrypt the data

exp: Symmetric encryption uses one shared secret key for both operations, which makes it fast but creates the problem of distributing that key securely. A related public and private key pair is the defining feature of asymmetric (public-key) encryption instead.

q: Which of the following is a public-key (asymmetric) encryption algorithm?

opts.A: AES
opts.B: 3DES
opts.C: RSA
opts.D: Blowfish

exp: RSA is a public-key algorithm built on a public/private key pair and is widely used for key exchange and digital signatures. AES, 3DES and Blowfish are all symmetric block ciphers that use a single shared key.

q: Full-disk encryption on an office laptop mainly protects

opts.A: data at rest, if the laptop is lost or stolen
opts.B: data in transit while the user browses the internet
opts.C: the laptop against malware infection
opts.D: email attachments after they leave the laptop

exp: Full-disk encryption keeps the stored contents unreadable to anyone who cannot supply the key, which is why it is the standard control against theft of a device. Protecting data in transit is the job of TLS or a VPN, and once the user has logged in the operating system sees files normally, so it is no defence against malware.

q: A digital certificate primarily binds

opts.A: a password to a user name
opts.B: an IP address to a MAC address
opts.C: a file to its hash value
opts.D: a public key to the identity of its owner

exp: A certificate is a signed statement from a trusted Certifying Authority that a particular public key belongs to a named person, organisation or server. Binding a file to its hash value is what a message digest or checksum does, and no certificate is required for that.

q: In India, the Certifying Authorities that issue Digital Signature Certificates are licensed and regulated by the

opts.A: Indian Computer Emergency Response Team (CERT-In)
opts.B: Controller of Certifying Authorities (CCA)
opts.C: Telecom Regulatory Authority of India (TRAI)
opts.D: Unique Identification Authority of India (UIDAI)

exp: The Controller of Certifying Authorities, established under the Information Technology Act, licenses and supervises the Certifying Authorities that issue Digital Signature Certificates in India. CERT-In is the incident-response agency and has no role in licensing Certifying Authorities.

q: A digital certificate that must be treated as invalid before its stated expiry date is published in the

opts.A: Certificate Revocation List (CRL)
opts.B: Certificate Signing Request
opts.C: root certificate store
opts.D: trusted certificate chain

exp: When a certificate is compromised or its holder leaves, the Certifying Authority revokes it and lists it in a Certificate Revocation List that verifiers can consult. A Certificate Signing Request runs in the opposite direction: it is the application a subscriber submits to obtain a certificate in the first place.

q: In a PKI, data that has been encrypted with a user's public key can be decrypted only with

opts.A: the same public key
opts.B: the Certifying Authority's public key
opts.C: that user's private key
opts.D: a shared session password agreed in advance

exp: The two keys of a pair are complementary, so what one key locks only its partner can unlock; anyone may encrypt with the freely published public key, but only the holder of the matching private key can read the result. The public key cannot decrypt its own output, which is exactly why it can be published.

q: Which component of a Public Key Infrastructure issues and digitally signs certificates?

opts.A: The Registration Authority
opts.B: The Certifying Authority
opts.C: The Certificate Revocation List
opts.D: The key escrow service

exp: The Certifying (Certificate) Authority is the trusted issuer: it signs each certificate with its own private key, and that signature is what relying parties verify. A Registration Authority only handles verification of the applicant's identity and forwards the request; it does not sign certificates.

q: When a user digitally signs a document, the signature is created using

opts.A: the recipient's public key
opts.B: a symmetric session key
opts.C: the recipient's private key
opts.D: the signer's own private key

exp: Signing is done with the signer's private key, and anyone can then verify the signature using the signer's public key from the certificate. The recipient's public key is used for confidentiality (encrypting a message to that recipient), which is a different operation from signing.

q: The main purpose of a vulnerability assessment is to

opts.A: identify and rank known security weaknesses in systems and applications
opts.B: restore service after an unplanned outage
opts.C: measure the peak bandwidth utilisation of the network
opts.D: verify that user software licences are valid

exp: A vulnerability assessment systematically discovers known weaknesses such as missing patches, weak configurations and default passwords, and prioritises them by severity so they can be remediated. Restoring service after an outage belongs to incident response and business continuity, not to assessment.

q: How does penetration testing differ from a vulnerability assessment?

opts.A: It is performed automatically by antivirus software
opts.B: It examines only physical security of the server room
opts.C: It actively attempts to exploit weaknesses to prove they can really be used
opts.D: It never makes use of automated tools

exp: A vulnerability assessment reports what appears weak, while a penetration test goes further and tries to exploit those weaknesses to demonstrate real, exploitable impact. Penetration testers do use automated tools; the distinction lies in active exploitation, not in the tooling.

q: Which of the following is commonly used as a vulnerability scanning tool?

opts.A: Wireshark
opts.B: Nessus
opts.C: FileZilla
opts.D: PuTTY

exp: Nessus is a well-known vulnerability scanner that probes hosts and reports missing patches and insecure configurations. Wireshark is a packet analyser used to capture and inspect network traffic, which helps in diagnosis but does not scan systems for vulnerabilities.

q: The main security purpose of patch management is to

opts.A: add new features requested by users
opts.B: increase the free disk space on servers
opts.C: reduce the electricity consumed by the data centre
opts.D: close known vulnerabilities by keeping software up to date

exp: Patch management is the controlled process of identifying, testing and deploying vendor fixes so that publicly known vulnerabilities are removed before attackers exploit them. Patches may sometimes add features as well, but that is incidental and not the security objective.

q: Why should a patch normally be applied in a test environment before it is rolled out to production servers?

opts.A: Because patches stop working after a fixed period
opts.B: Because testing reduces the download size of the patch
opts.C: Because a patch can break compatibility with existing applications
opts.D: Because vendors require written permission before installation

exp: A patch changes working software, so it can disrupt an in-house or legacy application; testing on a representative system first catches such breakage before it affects users. Testing has no effect on the patch's size, and no vendor permission is needed to install a released update.

q: Which Microsoft service allows an administrator to centrally approve and distribute Windows updates to computers on a local network?

opts.A: Windows Server Update Services (WSUS)
opts.B: Active Directory Domain Services
opts.C: Windows Defender Firewall
opts.D: Remote Desktop Services

exp: WSUS downloads updates once from Microsoft and lets the administrator approve and push them to client machines, saving bandwidth and giving control over what is installed. Active Directory Domain Services handles identity, authentication and directory objects, not update distribution.

q: In incident response, isolating an infected machine from the network so that the problem does not spread further is part of which phase?

opts.A: Eradication
opts.B: Recovery
opts.C: Lessons learned
opts.D: Containment

exp: Containment is the phase that limits the damage and stops the incident spreading, typically by disconnecting or segregating affected systems. Eradication comes afterwards and means actually removing the malware or closing the flaw that was exploited.

q: The national nodal agency for responding to computer security incidents in India is

opts.A: NIC
opts.B: CERT-In
opts.C: C-DAC
opts.D: STQC

exp: CERT-In, the Indian Computer Emergency Response Team, is the national nodal agency for cyber security incident reporting, alerts and coordinated response. NIC provides IT infrastructure and services to government departments, but it is not the incident-response nodal agency.

q: Why are system logs and disk images preserved while a security incident is being handled?

opts.A: To free up disk space on the affected server
opts.B: To improve the speed of the network after the attack
opts.C: To support forensic analysis and any later legal action
opts.D: To allow the antivirus to update its signature database

exp: Logs and forensic images are the evidence that shows how the attacker got in and what was touched, and they must be preserved intact for investigation and possible prosecution. Rebuilding a machine before capturing this evidence destroys it permanently, which is why preservation comes before cleanup.

q: Which of the following daily practices in a government office is an example of good cyber hygiene?

opts.A: Using one common login shared by all the staff of a section
opts.B: Turning off automatic security updates so that the computer never restarts during work
opts.C: Locking the workstation screen whenever the user leaves the desk
opts.D: Keeping the network password written on a slip pasted on the monitor

exp: Cyber hygiene means the routine habits that keep systems safe, and locking the screen stops anyone from using an already authenticated session. A shared login may look convenient but it destroys accountability, since no action can be traced to a particular user.

q: Why is it recommended that office staff do their day-to-day work from a standard (non-administrator) user account?

opts.A: Malware that runs in that session cannot easily install itself across the whole system
opts.B: The computer boots faster when a standard account is used
opts.C: Activity from standard accounts is not written to audit logs
opts.D: Antivirus software scans only standard user accounts

exp: Working with least privilege limits the damage of a successful attack, because system-wide changes need administrator rights that the session does not have. Standard accounts are logged just like any other; privilege level has nothing to do with whether activity is recorded.

q: A staff member receives an email claiming to be from the treasury and asking him to log in through a link. Which response best reflects good cyber hygiene?

opts.A: Reply to the mail asking the sender whether it is genuine
opts.B: Forward the mail to colleagues to get their opinion
opts.C: Open the attachment first to see whether it looks official
opts.D: Check the sender's actual address and reach the site by typing the known official URL instead of clicking the link

exp: Phishing works by getting the victim to follow the attacker's link, so verifying the sender and navigating independently to the known address defeats it. Replying is useless because a spoofed or attacker-controlled address will simply confirm that the mail is genuine.

q: Artificial Intelligence is best described as

opts.A: any software that stores and retrieves large volumes of data
opts.B: the branch of computer science concerned with building systems that perform tasks normally requiring human intelligence
opts.C: the technique of connecting computers so that they can exchange messages
opts.D: a method of increasing the clock speed of a processor

exp: AI is defined by the kind of task a system performs - perceiving, reasoning, learning, deciding, using language - not by the volume of data involved. Simply holding a large database is data management, not intelligence, because no inference or learning takes place.

q: An AI system built to do one specific job well, such as reading vehicle number plates from camera images, is described as

opts.A: General AI
opts.B: Super AI
opts.C: Narrow AI
opts.D: Autonomous AI

exp: Narrow AI, also called weak AI, is limited to the single task it was designed and trained for, and essentially all AI in practical use today is of this kind. General AI would mean a system able to transfer its ability across any intellectual task, which does not yet exist.

q: The Turing Test was proposed as a way of judging whether

opts.A: a machine can compute faster than a human being
opts.B: a program is free from logical errors
opts.C: a robot can find its way through an unknown environment
opts.D: a machine's replies in a conversation are indistinguishable from those of a human

exp: The test judges behaviour in conversation: if a human questioner cannot tell the machine's replies from a person's, the machine passes. Speed of calculation was never the criterion, since ordinary computers already far exceed humans at arithmetic without being called intelligent.

q: Which of the following is a supervised learning task?

opts.A: Classifying incoming email as spam or not spam, using a collection of emails already marked spam or not spam
opts.B: Grouping customers into segments when no group labels exist in the data
opts.C: Reducing the number of columns in a dataset while preserving most of its variation
opts.D: An agent learning to play a game by receiving rewards and penalties for its moves

exp: Supervised learning needs labelled examples, that is, inputs paired with the correct output, which is exactly what the pre-marked email collection provides. Grouping unlabelled customers is clustering, an unsupervised task, and learning from rewards is reinforcement learning.

q: In machine learning, 'overfitting' means that the model

opts.A: is too simple to capture the pattern present in the data
opts.B: fits the training data very closely but performs poorly on new, unseen data
opts.C: has been trained on too many different datasets at the same time
opts.D: gives the same output whatever input it is given

exp: An overfitted model has learned the noise and peculiarities of the training set instead of the general pattern, so its accuracy collapses on fresh data. A model that is too simple to capture the pattern is the opposite fault, underfitting.

q: Which type of machine learning is used when the data carries no labels and the aim is to discover natural groupings within it?

opts.A: Supervised learning
opts.B: Reinforcement learning
opts.C: Unsupervised learning
opts.D: Transfer learning

exp: Unsupervised learning works on unlabelled data and finds structure in it, clustering being its commonest form. Supervised learning cannot be used here at all, because it requires the correct answer to be supplied with every training example.

q: Deep learning is a form of machine learning that works through

opts.A: hand-written if-then rules maintained by domain experts
opts.B: spreadsheets linked together by formulas
opts.C: queries run against indexed relational database tables
opts.D: artificial neural networks having many layers of processing units

exp: The word 'deep' refers to the number of layers in the neural network, each layer building a more abstract representation than the one before. Systems driven by expert-written if-then rules are rule-based or expert systems, which do not learn from data at all.

q: On tasks such as image recognition, one practical advantage of deep learning over traditional machine learning is that

opts.A: it can learn the useful features directly from the raw data instead of needing features designed by hand
opts.B: it needs far less training data than traditional methods
opts.C: it always runs faster on an ordinary desktop processor
opts.D: its internal decisions are easier for a human to explain

exp: Deep networks learn their own feature representations from raw pixels, which removes much of the manual feature engineering that older methods required. The other options state the reverse of reality: deep learning is generally more data-hungry, more compute-hungry and harder to interpret.

q: Which piece of hardware is most commonly used to speed up the training of deep learning models?

opts.A: A larger capacity hard disk drive
opts.B: A graphics processing unit (GPU)
opts.C: A high-quality sound card
opts.D: A UPS of higher rating

exp: Training a neural network is largely repeated matrix arithmetic, and a GPU performs thousands of such operations in parallel, which is why GPUs (and similar accelerators) dominate this work. A bigger disk only helps in storing the dataset; it does not make the computation faster.

q: Natural Language Processing (NLP) is the field of AI concerned with

opts.A: converting analogue signals into digital form
opts.B: designing compilers for programming languages
opts.C: enabling computers to process, understand and generate human language
opts.D: translating machine code back into assembly language

exp: NLP covers tasks on ordinary human language such as translation, summarisation, question answering and sentiment analysis. Compiler design is a tempting choice but deals with formal artificial languages, which have a fixed unambiguous grammar unlike natural language.

q: In NLP, breaking up a piece of text into individual words or word-pieces before any further processing is called

opts.A: Tokenisation
opts.B: Summarisation
opts.C: Transcription
opts.D: Compression

exp: Tokenisation is the first step of most NLP pipelines and produces the tokens on which later stages operate. Summarisation shortens the meaning of a text and transcription converts spoken audio into text, so neither describes the splitting step.

q: A department processes thousands of citizen feedback messages to judge whether each one is positive, negative or neutral in tone. This NLP task is called

opts.A: Speech synthesis
opts.B: Named entity recognition
opts.C: Optical character recognition
opts.D: Sentiment analysis

exp: Sentiment analysis classifies text according to the opinion or emotion it expresses, which is exactly what judging tone amounts to. Named entity recognition also works on the same text but only pulls out names of persons, places and organisations; it says nothing about tone.

q: Computer vision is the branch of AI concerned with

opts.A: improving the resolution of computer monitors
opts.B: enabling computers to extract meaning from digital images and video
opts.C: designing attractive graphics for websites
opts.D: storing image files efficiently in a database

exp: Computer vision is about interpretation - recognising, locating and describing what appears in an image or video stream. Producing or displaying images is computer graphics and display technology, which is the reverse problem of understanding them.

q: In a traffic enforcement system, reading a vehicle's registration number out of a camera image relies mainly on

opts.A: text-to-speech conversion
opts.B: speech recognition
opts.C: optical character recognition
opts.D: data warehousing

exp: Optical character recognition converts the characters visible in an image into machine-readable text, which is what number-plate reading requires. Speech recognition is the analogous task for audio input and has no role where the input is a photograph.

q: A model that draws a box around every person visible in a CCTV frame and labels each box 'person' is performing

opts.A: object detection
opts.B: image classification
opts.C: image compression
opts.D: face verification

exp: Object detection both locates each instance with a bounding box and assigns it a class label. Image classification is the close distractor, but it gives a single label to the whole image without telling you where in the frame the object is.

q: Generative AI differs from traditional classification-type AI mainly in that it

opts.A: can run only on cloud servers and never on local hardware
opts.B: produces new content such as text, images, audio or code, instead of only classifying or predicting
opts.C: works without needing any training data at all
opts.D: always gives exactly the same output for the same input

exp: The defining feature of generative AI is that its output is fresh content rather than a label, score or category. It is still trained on very large quantities of existing data, so the claim that it needs no training data is false.

q: Which of the following is the best example of using generative AI in office work?

opts.A: Sorting a spreadsheet of applications by date of receipt
opts.B: Checking whether a password meets the complexity rules
opts.C: Blocking incoming traffic from a blacklisted IP address
opts.D: Producing a first draft of an office note from a few bullet points

exp: Drafting new prose from an outline is content creation, which is precisely what a generative model does. Sorting, rule-checking and traffic blocking are ordinary deterministic operations that conventional software has always handled without any AI.

q: Why must the output of a generative AI tool be checked by a human before it is placed on an official file?

opts.A: It can produce fluent, confident text that is factually wrong or entirely invented
opts.B: It always answers in a language other than the one requested
opts.C: Its output cannot be copied into a word processor
opts.D: It refuses to produce more than one paragraph at a time

exp: Generative models optimise for plausible-sounding output, not verified truth, so wrong facts, invented references and outdated rules can appear stated with full confidence. Fluency is what makes this dangerous, because the error carries no visible warning sign.

q: A Large Language Model (LLM) is trained mainly to

opts.A: store documents so that they can be searched by keyword
opts.B: convert SQL queries into printed report formats
opts.C: predict the most likely continuation of a piece of text, having been trained on very large quantities of text
opts.D: compress text files so that they occupy less storage

exp: An LLM learns statistical patterns of language by repeatedly predicting the next token in text, and its abilities in answering, summarising and drafting emerge from that objective. It is not a document store, and it does not retrieve a saved copy of any text it was trained on.

q: In the context of LLMs, the term 'hallucination' refers to a situation where

opts.A: the model refuses to answer the question put to it
opts.B: the model produces information that sounds plausible but is false or invented
opts.C: the model's reply is delayed because of network congestion
opts.D: the model repeats the user's question back word for word

exp: A hallucination is confidently asserted content with no basis in fact, such as a non-existent circular number or a made-up citation. A refusal to answer is a different behaviour altogether and is usually a safety or policy response, not a hallucination.

q: What is meant by the 'context window' of a large language model?

opts.A: The area of the screen in which the chat conversation is displayed
opts.B: The period for which the vendor retains the user's conversation history
opts.C: The number of users who may query the model at the same time
opts.D: The amount of text the model can take into account at one time

exp: The context window is the limit on how much text - prompt, attached material and the reply being generated - the model can consider together, and material beyond it is effectively out of view. It is a property of the model, not of the user interface or of the vendor's data-retention policy.

q: Prompt engineering is best described as

opts.A: writing and refining the instructions given to an AI model so that it produces more useful output
opts.B: modifying the model's source code to change how it behaves
opts.C: training the model again on the organisation's own data
opts.D: reducing the size of a model so that it will run on a laptop

exp: Prompt engineering works entirely through the input given to the model, by stating the task, context, format and constraints clearly. Retraining on the organisation's own data is fine-tuning, which changes the model itself and is a quite different exercise.

q: Placing two or three worked examples inside the prompt so that the model can infer the pattern required is known as

opts.A: Zero-shot prompting
opts.B: Fine-tuning
opts.C: Few-shot prompting
opts.D: Chain-of-thought prompting

exp: Few-shot prompting supplies a handful of input-output examples in the prompt itself, leaving the model's weights untouched. Zero-shot prompting gives the instruction with no examples, and fine-tuning would involve actually retraining the model on example data.

q: A user gets poor results from the vague prompt 'write about our office'. Which is the most effective way to improve it?

opts.A: Repeat the same prompt several times until a good answer happens to appear
opts.B: State the purpose, the intended reader, the required length and the format wanted
opts.C: Type the whole prompt in capital letters for emphasis
opts.D: Add a request that the model answer as quickly as possible

exp: A good prompt removes ambiguity by specifying task, audience, scope and output format, which leaves the model far less to guess. Merely repeating a vague prompt changes nothing about the instruction and only produces different guesses.

q: Bias in an AI model most commonly arises from

opts.A: the speed of the processor used during training
opts.B: the use of too many programming languages in the codebase
opts.C: storing the trained model on a public cloud server
opts.D: training data that under-represents some groups or reflects past unfair practice

exp: A model learns the patterns present in its training data, so historical imbalance or discrimination in that data is reproduced and often amplified in its predictions. Hardware speed and choice of programming language affect cost and maintainability, not fairness of the output.

q: Which of the following reflects the approach to Responsible AI set out by NITI Aayog for India?

opts.A: Safety and reliability, inclusiveness and non-discrimination, privacy, transparency and accountability in the design and use of AI
opts.B: Compulsory adoption of AI by every government department within a fixed deadline
opts.C: A prohibition on private sector participation in AI research
opts.D: A preference for the largest available model in every application

exp: NITI Aayog's Responsible AI approach is a set of principles about how AI should be built and used - safely, inclusively, transparently and with clear accountability, while protecting privacy. It is guidance on responsible practice, not a mandate to deploy AI everywhere or a restriction on who may do AI research.

q: An office wishes to use an AI tool on citizens' personal data. Under the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023, it is primarily expected to

opts.A: publish the personal data on its website in the interest of transparency
opts.B: retain all the personal data indefinitely so that audit is possible
opts.C: process the data only for a lawful purpose, normally with the individual's consent, and keep it secure
opts.D: hand the data over to the AI vendor as a condition of using the tool

exp: The Act requires personal data to be processed for a lawful purpose on the basis of consent or a permitted legitimate use, with the data fiduciary responsible for security safeguards and for not keeping data longer than needed. Publishing personal data would breach the very confidentiality the law is meant to protect.

q: Which of the following is the Government of India's national initiative for building up the country's artificial intelligence ecosystem?

opts.A: BharatNet
opts.B: IndiaAI
opts.C: UMANG
opts.D: GeM

exp: IndiaAI is the national mission covering AI compute capacity, datasets, skilling, startups and safe and trusted AI. The others are genuine government programmes in different areas: BharatNet for rural broadband, UMANG as a unified mobile app for government services, and GeM for public procurement.

q: A state government adds an AI chatbot to its citizen services portal. The main benefit expected is that it

opts.A: removes the need to keep the underlying service records accurate
opts.B: makes protection of citizens' personal data unnecessary
opts.C: replaces the legal requirement of a signed application
opts.D: answers routine, repetitive queries at any hour, letting staff concentrate on complex cases

exp: The value of such a chatbot lies in handling high-volume standard questions instantly and round the clock, which shortens waiting and frees staff for cases needing judgement. It changes none of the underlying obligations - accurate records, data protection and prescribed procedure all continue to apply.

q: In a government office, which of these tasks is LEAST suitable to be left to an AI system without human review?

opts.A: Taking the final decision to reject a citizen's application for a welfare benefit
opts.B: Sorting incoming letters into likely departments for a clerk to confirm
opts.C: Suggesting a first draft of a reply for an officer to edit
opts.D: Flagging unusually large bills so that an auditor can examine them

exp: A decision that affects a citizen's rights or entitlement needs a human decision-maker who can give reasons and be held answerable on appeal, so AI may assist but must not decide. In the other three the AI only sorts, drafts or flags, and a human official remains the one who decides.

q: In IT operations, the term 'AIOps' refers to:

opts.A: A scripting language used to automate server maintenance jobs
opts.B: A hardware appliance that replaces the network firewall
opts.C: The use of artificial intelligence and machine learning on operations data such as logs, metrics and alerts
opts.D: A rule requiring every server to be rebooted on a fixed schedule

exp: AIOps applies machine learning to the large volume of monitoring data an IT estate produces, so that alerts can be correlated and faults diagnosed faster. It is an approach to analysing operations data, not a scripting language or a physical appliance.

q: A monitoring tool learns a server's usual CPU and network usage pattern and raises an alert when current behaviour departs sharply from that pattern. This is an example of:

opts.A: Load balancing
opts.B: Anomaly detection
opts.C: Patch management
opts.D: Disk defragmentation

exp: Anomaly detection builds a baseline of normal behaviour and flags statistically unusual deviations from it, which is why it catches problems no fixed threshold was written for. Load balancing only distributes traffic; it never judges whether behaviour is unusual.

q: An AI assistant suggests a command to free up disk space on a production server. What is the correct practice for a System Manager?

opts.A: Run it at once, since AI suggestions are pre-validated by the tool vendor
opts.B: Run it on the busiest day of the month so the benefit is clearly visible
opts.C: Forward it to users so that each of them runs it on their own machine
opts.D: Review and test the suggested command first, with the administrator remaining accountable for the result

exp: AI suggestions are generated without full knowledge of the local environment and can be wrong or destructive, so a human must review, test and stay answerable for what is executed. Vendors do not validate individual generated outputs.

q: Which Microsoft Excel feature examines a selected range of data and automatically suggests trends, patterns and ready-made charts?

opts.A: Analyze Data (earlier called 'Ideas')
opts.B: Goal Seek
opts.C: Flash Fill
opts.D: Freeze Panes

exp: Analyze Data scans the selected range and proposes summaries, trends and suggested visualisations in plain language. Goal Seek works backwards from a target value in a single formula and does not describe a dataset at all.

q: An officer types 'show total expenditure district-wise for last year' into a reporting tool and it produces the corresponding chart. This capability is called:

opts.A: Macro recording
opts.B: Data validation
opts.C: Natural language query
opts.D: Conditional formatting

exp: Natural language query lets the user ask a question in ordinary words, which the tool translates into a query against the dataset and renders as a result or chart. Macro recording can only replay steps that were recorded earlier.

q: An AI tool produces a summary, with totals, of a departmental expenditure sheet. Before those figures go into an official note, the System Manager should:

opts.A: Accept them as final, because the tool read the actual file
opts.B: Verify the figures against the source data, because AI tools can state plausible but incorrect numbers
opts.C: Delete the source file so that two versions of the data do not exist
opts.D: Convert the summary into an image so that it cannot be edited

exp: Generative AI can produce confident-sounding but wrong figures, so any number destined for an official record must be reconciled with the source. Having read the file is no guarantee that the arithmetic or the interpretation is right.

q: The eOffice product suite used by Indian government offices is developed by:

opts.A: National Informatics Centre (NIC)
opts.B: Unique Identification Authority of India (UIDAI)
opts.C: Telecom Regulatory Authority of India (TRAI)
opts.D: National Payments Corporation of India (NPCI)

exp: eOffice is a product of the National Informatics Centre, the government's IT services organisation under the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology. UIDAI runs Aadhaar and NPCI runs payment systems such as UPI; neither builds office automation software.

q: Which module of NIC eOffice handles electronic receipts, electronic files and noting?

opts.A: KMS
opts.B: eFile
opts.C: eLeave
opts.D: CAMS

exp: eFile is the file management module: it diarises receipts, creates and moves electronic files, records notes and handles drafts and dispatch. KMS is the knowledge repository, eLeave handles leave applications and CAMS provides messaging and collaboration.

q: Which eOffice module maintains employee personnel and service record information?

opts.A: eFile
opts.B: KMS
opts.C: CAMS
opts.D: PIMS

exp: PIMS, the Personnel Information Management System, holds employee master and service-record data that other modules such as eLeave draw upon. eFile deals with files and receipts, not with establishment records.

sub: e-Office Concept and Digital Office Environment
q: What is the main objective of the e-Office initiative in government offices?

opts.A: To provide free internet connectivity to every government employee
opts.B: To host the department's public website and social media accounts
opts.C: To shift file handling and decision-making from paper to a transparent, traceable electronic workflow
opts.D: To computerise salary and pension payments only

exp: e-Office replaces the manual movement of dak and files with an electronic workflow that is faster, traceable and auditable end to end. Payroll and pension computerisation is a separate class of application and not the purpose of e-Office.

sub: e-Office Concept and Digital Office Environment
q: In an e-Office environment, a 'receipt' means:

opts.A: An incoming communication (dak) that has been diarised in the system
opts.B: An acknowledgement issued to a party after a payment is made
opts.C: A remark recorded by an officer on a file
opts.D: A letter issued by the office to an outside party

exp: Incoming dak is scanned and diarised, at which point it becomes an electronic receipt that can be marked to an officer or attached to a file. An officer's remark is a note, and an outgoing communication is an issue or dispatch.

sub: e-Office Concept and Digital Office Environment
q: The e-Office programme is often described as creating a 'less paper office'. This wording means that:

opts.A: Paper files become legally invalid once e-Office is installed
opts.B: Printing is permitted only on both sides of the sheet
opts.C: Files may be created electronically but must still be moved physically for approval
opts.D: Dependence on paper is progressively reduced as more work shifts to the electronic system

exp: 'Less paper' is deliberate wording: the aim is a steady reduction in paper as processes move online, while some documents legitimately continue to exist on paper. Nothing in e-Office invalidates paper records outright.

q: The Knowledge Management System (KMS) module of eOffice is primarily used to:

opts.A: Apply for and sanction leave online
opts.B: Maintain a central, searchable repository of Acts, rules, circulars and guidelines
opts.C: Exchange instant messages between officers
opts.D: Record annual performance appraisals of officers

exp: KMS is the department's shared document repository, holding reference material such as Acts, rules, office memoranda and circulars for authorised users to search. Leave is handled by eLeave and messaging by CAMS.

q: How is content typically organised in the eOffice Knowledge Management System?

opts.A: As a single flat list ordered only by the time of upload
opts.B: As one compressed archive file for each financial year
opts.C: Under a hierarchy of categories and sub-categories, with access controlled by role
opts.D: Inside each officer's personal mailbox

exp: KMS arranges documents in a category and sub-category tree with role-based permissions and search, so an officer can locate the right circular quickly. A flat list ordered by upload time would defeat the whole purpose of retrieval.

q: Which benefit is most directly associated with a Knowledge Management System in a government department?

opts.A: Institutional memory is preserved, so knowledge is not lost when officers are transferred
opts.B: Files move automatically to the next officer without being marked
opts.C: Salary bills are generated without any manual data entry
opts.D: The office needs less internet bandwidth than before

exp: A KMS captures rules, precedents and guidance in a shared repository, so an incoming officer can find them instead of depending on a predecessor's personal papers. Automatic movement of files is a workflow feature of eFile, not of KMS.

q: Role-based access control in eOffice means that:

opts.A: Every user can open every file, but all actions are logged
opts.B: A user's rights are determined by the post and role assigned to that user
opts.C: Access is granted in proportion to the user's length of service
opts.D: Each user selects the required access rights from a settings menu

exp: Rights follow the post and role mapped to a user, so a change of posting automatically changes what that person can see and do. Users cannot grant rights to themselves, and open access to all files would defeat the control entirely.

q: What is the main purpose of the audit trail maintained by eOffice for each file?

opts.A: To compress older files so that they occupy less storage
opts.B: To keep a spare copy in case the server fails
opts.C: To translate notes into regional languages
opts.D: To record who acted on the file, what action was taken and when

exp: The audit trail is a chronological, tamper-evident history of every action on a file, which is what makes accountability and non-repudiation possible. Backup and compression are storage functions and establish nothing about who did what.

q: An officer is proceeding on two weeks' leave, and files marked to that post must continue to be processed. The correct approach is to:

opts.A: Share the eOffice password with a trusted colleague
opts.B: Hand over the DSC token along with its PIN to the section assistant
opts.C: Use the delegation facility so that files reach the officer holding charge
opts.D: Ask users to email documents directly instead of using eOffice

exp: Delegation passes the workload to the officer holding charge while keeping every action attributable to the person who actually took it. Sharing a password or a signing token destroys non-repudiation and is a serious security breach.

q: In India, a Digital Signature Certificate is issued by:

opts.A: A Certifying Authority licensed by the Controller of Certifying Authorities under the Information Technology Act
opts.B: Any commercial bank in which the applicant holds an account
opts.C: The office or department in which the applicant is employed
opts.D: The Registrar of Companies of the applicant's state

exp: DSCs are issued only by licensed Certifying Authorities, which operate under the Controller of Certifying Authorities established by the Information Technology Act, 2000. Employers, banks and the Registrar of Companies may require a DSC but cannot issue one.

q: When a document is digitally signed using a DSC, which key is used for signing and which for verification?

opts.A: The signer's public key signs, and the signer's private key verifies
opts.B: The signer's private key signs, and the signer's public key verifies
opts.C: The recipient's public key signs, and the recipient's private key verifies
opts.D: One shared secret key is used both to sign and to verify

exp: Only the signer holds the private key, so only the signer can create the signature, while anyone can verify it using the public key carried in the certificate. A shared secret key could not prove which of the parties signed.

q: A note in eOffice is approved by signing it with a Digital Signature Certificate. What does that digital signature primarily assure?

opts.A: That the note cannot be read by anyone other than the addressee
opts.B: That the note will be delivered within a fixed time limit
opts.C: That the note genuinely came from the signer and has not been altered since signing
opts.D: That the note has been backed up on the departmental server

exp: A digital signature provides authentication of the signer, integrity of the content and non-repudiation of the act of signing. Keeping the content secret from others is encryption, which is a different use of the same key pair.

q: In eOffice, a workflow is best described as:

opts.A: The bandwidth allotted to each section of the office
opts.B: The list of reference documents stored in the knowledge repository
opts.C: The timetable on which the server is backed up
opts.D: The defined sequence of officers and steps through which a receipt or file moves for noting and approval

exp: A workflow is the configured route and set of steps a receipt or file follows, level by level, up to the competent authority and back. The stored reference documents are KMS content and have nothing to do with routing.

q: Which of the following is a workflow configuration task for an eOffice administrator?

opts.A: Mapping employees to posts and sections in the organisational hierarchy so that files can be marked to a post
opts.B: Drafting the reply letter to be issued on a file
opts.C: Recording the officer's remarks in the note portion of a file
opts.D: Scanning the incoming letter at the receipt counter

exp: Administrators set up the master data — sections, posts and the employee-to-post mapping — that determines where a file can be routed. Drafting, noting and scanning are day-to-day user actions performed within the workflow, not configuration of it.

q: Setting a time limit after which a file still pending with an officer is highlighted to a higher authority is an example of configuring:

opts.A: A metadata standard
opts.B: A record retention schedule
opts.C: An escalation or pendency rule in the workflow
opts.D: A digital signature policy

exp: Escalation rules convert elapsed time into a management alert, so that files held beyond the permitted period surface for review instead of lying unnoticed. A retention schedule governs how long closed records are kept and says nothing about pendency.

q: Metadata is best defined as:

opts.A: A backup copy of a document kept on a separate server
opts.B: Data that describes other data, such as its title, author, date and category
opts.C: Data that has been encrypted for secure transmission
opts.D: The temporary data held in a computer's main memory

exp: Metadata is descriptive information about a resource — who created it, when, and under what subject — and it is what makes the resource findable and manageable. An encrypted copy is still the data itself, not a description of it.

q: Which of the following is metadata of an electronic file in eOffice, rather than its content?

opts.A: The scanned copy of the letter received from a member of the public
opts.B: The file number, subject and category assigned to the file
opts.C: The remarks recorded by the officer in the note
opts.D: The draft reply prepared for approval

exp: The file number, subject and category describe the file and are what the system uses to index, search and route it. The scanned letter, the notes and the draft are the substantive content that the file carries.

q: Why do e-governance projects insist on common metadata standards across departments?

opts.A: Because they reduce the storage space each document occupies
opts.B: Because they remove the need to sign documents digitally
opts.C: Because they increase the speed of the office internet connection
opts.D: Because consistent description makes records reliably searchable and lets different systems exchange data

exp: When every department describes a record in the same way, search results become dependable and data can pass between systems without manual re-keying, which is the aim of the government's metadata and data standards work. Metadata does not compress files or affect bandwidth.

q: A record retention schedule is:

opts.A: A statement of how long each class of record must be kept before it is destroyed or transferred to archives
opts.B: A list of officers authorised to sign outgoing letters
opts.C: The timetable on which the file server is backed up each night
opts.D: A register of the files currently pending with each section

exp: A retention schedule assigns a retention period to each category of record, so that weeding and archiving follow a rule rather than individual judgement. A backup timetable protects against data loss and is an entirely separate control.

q: Public records of the Central Government that are of permanent value are ultimately transferred to the custody of:

opts.A: The National Informatics Centre
opts.B: The Central Information Commission
opts.C: The National Archives of India
opts.D: The Comptroller and Auditor General of India

exp: Under the Public Records Act, the National Archives of India is the custodian of non-current Central Government records of permanent value. The Central Information Commission decides RTI appeals and the CAG audits accounts; neither is a records repository.

q: How does an archive differ from a backup?

opts.A: There is no difference; the two terms mean the same thing
opts.B: A backup must be kept offline, whereas an archive must always remain online
opts.C: A backup keeps records permanently, whereas an archive is deleted every year
opts.D: A backup is a copy kept to recover from failure or loss, while an archive is long-term retention of records that have lasting value

exp: Backups exist to restore recent working data after a failure and are overwritten in cycles, whereas archives preserve records of enduring value for as long as the retention rules require. Treating backups as an archive risks losing records when the backup cycle rolls over.

q: In a digital office, an incoming letter has just been scanned at the central registry. What is the next step in office procedure?

opts.A: It is diarised in the system, creating an electronic receipt
opts.B: It is dispatched to an addressee outside the office
opts.C: It is recorded and assigned a retention category
opts.D: It is signed with a Digital Signature Certificate by the dealing hand

exp: Scanning is followed by diarisation, which registers the communication as a receipt that can then be marked to an officer or attached to a file. Recording happens only at the other end of the process, when action on a file is complete.

q: In office procedure, the part of a file that carries the officers' remarks, analysis and recommendations on the issue under consideration is called the:

opts.A: Correspondence portion
opts.B: Note portion
opts.C: Appendix to correspondence
opts.D: Dispatch register

exp: The note portion holds the successive notes recorded by officers as a case moves up for decision, while the correspondence portion holds the letters received and issued. The dispatch register records outgoing communications and is not part of the file.

q: In office procedure, 'recording' a file means:

opts.A: Marking the file to a senior officer for orders
opts.B: Entering an incoming letter in the diary
opts.C: Closing the file after action on it is complete and assigning it a retention category
opts.D: Making a photocopy of the file for the section's reference

exp: Recording is the closing action: once the issues in a file have been disposed of, the file is closed, indexed and categorised so that its retention period is fixed. Entering an incoming letter is diarisation, which happens at the start of the process.

q: What is the main purpose of a service desk in IT Service Management?

opts.A: To design the physical layout of the server room
opts.B: To write the source code of the organisation's business applications
opts.C: To act as the single point of contact between users and the IT organisation
opts.D: To negotiate hardware purchase prices with vendors

exp: A service desk exists so that users have one known place to report faults, raise requests and get status updates, and so that all such contacts are logged and tracked. Negotiating with vendors is procurement work, not the service desk's function.

q: IT Service Management (ITSM) is best described as

opts.A: managing IT end to end as a set of services delivered to meet the needs of the business
opts.B: installing and configuring operating systems on user desktops
opts.C: writing the technical manuals that accompany IT equipment
opts.D: monitoring only the network hardware of an organisation

exp: ITSM takes a service view of IT: what the organisation receives is a service with an agreed quality, and the technology, people and processes behind it are managed to deliver that service. Installing desktop operating systems is one technical activity inside ITSM, not a definition of it.

q: In ITIL practice, what distinguishes a problem from an incident?

opts.A: A problem is reported by a user, while an incident is detected only by monitoring tools
opts.B: An incident is a single disruption of service that must be restored, while a problem is the underlying cause that must be eliminated
opts.C: A problem always affects only one user, while an incident affects many users
opts.D: An incident must be recorded in writing, while a problem is handled verbally

exp: Incident handling aims at restoring normal service as quickly as possible, even by a temporary workaround, whereas problem handling investigates why the incidents keep happening and removes the cause. Both incidents and problems may be raised by users or by monitoring, so the source is not the distinction.

q: Within ITIL, the main purpose of change management is to

opts.A: restore normal service as quickly as possible after an outage
opts.B: maintain a record of every hardware item owned by the organisation
opts.C: measure how satisfied users are with the service desk
opts.D: ensure that changes to IT services are assessed, authorised and implemented in a controlled way

exp: Change management exists to reduce the risk that a modification to a live service causes an unplanned outage, by requiring assessment, authorisation, scheduling and a fallback plan. Restoring service quickly after an outage is incident management, a separate practice.

q: IT Asset Management is primarily concerned with

opts.A: tracking and managing IT assets through their whole lifecycle, from acquisition through use to disposal
opts.B: writing user manuals for newly purchased equipment
opts.C: encrypting the data stored on organisational servers
opts.D: training staff to use office productivity software

exp: IT Asset Management covers the full lifecycle of hardware and software assets: planning and purchase, deployment, maintenance, and secure disposal or write-off. Encrypting stored data is an information security control and is not what asset management is for.

q: Which of the following is the strongest reason for an office to maintain an up-to-date IT asset register?

opts.A: It removes the need to install antivirus software on the machines listed
opts.B: It guarantees that the listed hardware will not fail
opts.C: It records what equipment the office owns, where each item is and who is accountable for it
opts.D: It increases the speed of the office network

exp: An asset register answers what, where and whose, which is what makes maintenance, audit, insurance and eventual disposal possible. Recording a machine in a register does nothing to protect it from malware or from hardware failure.

q: Software Asset Management is chiefly concerned with

opts.A: designing the user interface of software developed in house
opts.B: managing software licences and entitlements so that actual use stays within what has been purchased
opts.C: physically labelling desktop computers with inventory numbers
opts.D: repairing faulty printers and scanners

exp: Software Asset Management is the licensing and compliance side of asset management: knowing what is installed, what has been bought, and whether the two agree. Attaching inventory labels to hardware belongs to physical IT asset management.

q: An office has purchased 40 licences of a software package but has installed it on 55 computers. This situation is best described as

opts.A: over-licensing, in which money has been wasted on unused licences
opts.B: a backup failure
opts.C: a document version control problem
opts.D: under-licensing, a compliance breach that can expose the office to penalties on audit

exp: Installations exceed entitlements, so 15 copies are being used without a licence, which is exactly what a vendor or departmental audit penalises. Over-licensing is the opposite failure, where far more licences are bought than are ever installed, and it wastes money rather than creating legal exposure.

q: The main aim of Business Continuity Planning is to

opts.A: ensure that the organisation's essential functions can continue during and after a serious disruption
opts.B: replace all IT equipment on a fixed five-year cycle
opts.C: recover files that a user has accidentally deleted
opts.D: reduce the cost of purchasing new software licences

exp: Business continuity planning identifies the functions the organisation cannot stop performing and arranges alternative staff, premises, suppliers and procedures to keep them going. Recovering an individual deleted file is routine support work, not the subject of a continuity plan.

q: How does Business Continuity Planning differ from Disaster Recovery Planning?

opts.A: Business continuity applies only to natural disasters, while disaster recovery applies only to cyber attacks
opts.B: Business continuity covers keeping the organisation's overall functions running, while disaster recovery focuses on restoring IT systems and data
opts.C: Business continuity is prepared only after an incident, while disaster recovery is prepared before it
opts.D: Business continuity is the vendor's responsibility, while disaster recovery is the customer's

exp: Business continuity is the wider organisational discipline, covering people, premises, processes and suppliers, and disaster recovery is the IT-focused part of it that restores systems, applications and data. Both are prepared in advance, and both apply to any cause of disruption, whether natural, technical or malicious.

q: In a disaster recovery plan, the Recovery Time Objective (RTO) specifies

opts.A: the amount of data, measured as a period of work, that the organisation can afford to lose
opts.B: the number of backup copies that must be kept at an off-site location
opts.C: the maximum acceptable time for which a service may remain unavailable before it is restored
opts.D: the total cost of rebuilding the data centre after a disaster

exp: RTO is a downtime target: it states how long the organisation can function without the service before the consequences become unacceptable, and it drives the choice of standby arrangements. The amount of tolerable data loss is the Recovery Point Objective, a separate measure.

q: An office states that if its server fails it can afford to lose at most one hour of data. This statement defines the office's

opts.A: Recovery Time Objective
opts.B: Mean Time Between Failures
opts.C: Service Level Agreement uptime percentage
opts.D: Recovery Point Objective

exp: The Recovery Point Objective is the maximum tolerable data loss expressed as a period of time, and it determines how frequently backups or replication must run, here at least hourly. The Recovery Time Objective would instead state how long the office can remain without the server.

q: GeM, widely used by government departments in India, is

opts.A: an online marketplace portal through which government buyers procure goods and services
opts.B: a software licence audit tool supplied to state departments
opts.C: a national register of serving government employees
opts.D: a standard format for writing technical specifications

exp: The Government e-Marketplace is an online platform where registered sellers list goods and services and government buyers place orders, with the aim of making public purchasing faster and more transparent. It is a buying platform, not an audit tool or a personnel database.

q: In a two-bid tender for IT equipment, a bidder's financial bid is normally opened only when

opts.A: the bidder has supplied to the same department before
opts.B: the bidder's technical bid has been evaluated and found to meet the required specifications
opts.C: the bidder quoted the lowest price in an earlier tender
opts.D: the bidder submits a bank guarantee after the closing date

exp: The two-bid system keeps price hidden until technical suitability has been judged, so that the evaluation of specifications cannot be influenced by the quoted amount. Past supply to the department is not by itself a ground for opening the financial bid.

q: Why should official IT documents carry a version number and a date?

opts.A: It reduces the file size of the document
opts.B: It prevents the document from being printed
opts.C: It makes clear which revision is current, so that readers do not act on a superseded copy
opts.D: It encrypts the contents of the document automatically

exp: Versioning and dating let anyone holding a copy tell whether it is the latest one, which matters when procedures, configurations or contact details change. Version information has no effect on file size, printing or security.

q: What is the main benefit of following an organisation-wide documentation standard?

opts.A: Documents can be produced faster because no review is required
opts.B: Documents automatically become legally binding contracts
opts.C: Documents no longer need to be retained once a project ends
opts.D: Documents share a consistent structure and style, so any reader can locate information quickly

exp: A documentation standard fixes the expected sections, headings, terminology and layout, so a reader who knows the standard can find the needed information in any document without relearning its arrangement. Standards do not remove the need for review or for retaining records.

q: The 'triple constraint' commonly referred to in project management is the balance between

opts.A: scope, time and cost
opts.B: people, process and technology
opts.C: risk, reward and reputation
opts.D: hardware, software and network

exp: Scope, time and cost are interlinked, so enlarging the scope of a project normally forces either the schedule or the budget to grow, and quality suffers if neither is allowed to move. People, process and technology is a general management triad, not the project constraint model.

q: Which statement best distinguishes a project from routine operations?

opts.A: A project involves computers, while operations do not
opts.B: A project is a temporary effort with a defined start, end and deliverable, while operations are ongoing and repetitive
opts.C: A project is always carried out by an external vendor
opts.D: A project has no budget limit, while operations always do

exp: A project is temporary and produces a unique result, such as rolling out a new office network, after which it closes; operations are the continuing day-to-day running of that network. Projects may be executed in house and are certainly bound by a budget.

q: In a technical report, the executive summary is intended to

opts.A: list every source consulted while preparing the report
opts.B: present the detailed calculations that support the findings
opts.C: give the reader a short overview of the purpose, main findings and recommendations
opts.D: record the names of everyone who worked on the report

exp: An executive summary is written for a senior reader who may not read the whole report, so it condenses why the work was done, what was found and what is recommended. Detailed calculations belong in the body or the appendices, and sources belong in the references.

q: Detailed data tables, raw survey forms and long configuration listings that support a technical report are best placed

opts.A: in the introduction
opts.B: inside the executive summary
opts.C: in the covering letter
opts.D: in an appendix at the end of the report

exp: Supporting material is put in an appendix so that the main text stays readable while the evidence remains available to anyone who wants to check it. Placing bulk data in the executive summary defeats its purpose of being brief.

q: In official email, the Bcc field should be used when

opts.A: the addresses of some recipients must be kept hidden from the other recipients
opts.B: the message needs to reach the recipient more quickly
opts.C: the message must be marked as high priority
opts.D: the sender wants a delivery receipt for the message

exp: Recipients placed in Bcc receive the message but their addresses are not shown to anyone else, which is why it is used for large circulars where addresses should not be disclosed. Bcc has no bearing on delivery speed, priority marking or receipts.

q: Why should an official government email be drafted as carefully as a formal letter?

opts.A: Because an email cannot be deleted once it has been sent
opts.B: Because official email is an official record and may later be produced in an audit or an inquiry
opts.C: Because email is automatically published on the department's website
opts.D: Because email software refuses to send informal language

exp: Official correspondence sent by email forms part of the office record and can be called for during audit, inspection or an information request, so its tone, accuracy and completeness matter. Email is certainly deletable and is not published automatically anywhere.

q: Which document is normally circulated to members before an official meeting, listing the items to be taken up and the order in which they will be discussed?

opts.A: Minutes
opts.B: Agenda
opts.C: Action Taken Report
opts.D: Attendance sheet

exp: The agenda is prepared and circulated in advance so members know what will be discussed and can come prepared. Minutes are the opposite in timing — they are written after the meeting to record what was decided.

q: Minutes of an official meeting are primarily expected to record:

opts.A: A word-for-word transcript of everything each member said
opts.B: Only the names and designations of those who attended
opts.C: The decisions taken and the action points with the officer responsible for each
opts.D: The chairperson's personal assessment of each member's contribution

exp: Minutes are a summary record of outcomes — decisions, action points with owners and timelines, along with attendance and apologies for absence. They are deliberately not a verbatim transcript; capturing every spoken word is the job of proceedings or a recording, not of minutes.

q: The number of applications processed at a district e-District centre rose from 1,250 in 2024 to 1,500 in 2025. The percentage increase is:
exp: The rise is 1,500 - 1,250 = 250, and percentage increase is taken on the original value: 250 / 1,250 x 100 = 20%. Dividing 250 by the new figure 1,500 gives 16.67%, which is the common error — percentage increase is always measured against the earlier value.

q: A department's internet bills for five successive months were Rs 8,000, Rs 9,500, Rs 7,000, Rs 10,500 and Rs 10,000. The average monthly bill was:
exp: The five bills total 8,000 + 9,500 + 7,000 + 10,500 + 10,000 = Rs 45,000, and 45,000 / 5 = Rs 9,000. Rs 9,500 is the middle value when the figures are arranged in order, which is the median, not the average.

q: Find the next term in the series: 5, 11, 23, 47, ___
exp: Each term is double the previous term plus one: 5x2+1 = 11, 11x2+1 = 23, 23x2+1 = 47, so the next term is 47x2+1 = 95. Simply doubling gives 94 and doubling with no adjustment does not reproduce the earlier terms.

q: In a certain code, COMPUTER is written as DPNQVUFS. In the same code, PRINTER will be written as:

opts.A: QSJOUFS
opts.B: OQHMSDQ
opts.C: QSJOUFR
opts.D: QSJNUFS

exp: Each letter of the word is replaced by the next letter of the alphabet (C to D, O to P, M to N, and so on), so PRINTER becomes Q, S, J, O, U, F, S — that is QSJOUFS. OQHMSDQ is what you get by moving one letter backwards instead of forwards.

q: An officer asks an AI chatbot about a welfare scheme, and the reply confidently cites an office memorandum with a number and date that do not exist in any departmental record. This behaviour of a generative AI model is known as:

opts.A: Prompt injection
opts.B: Data mining
opts.C: Overfitting
opts.D: Hallucination

exp: A hallucination is output that is fluent and plausible-looking but factually invented, such as a fabricated citation, circular number or case reference. Prompt injection is different — it is an attack in which hidden instructions in the input make the model behave against its operator's intent.

q: An AI tool produces a fluent, confidently worded summary of a 40-page tender document. Before circulating the summary to the tender committee, the System Manager should:

opts.A: Accept it as it is, because the language is fluent and free of hesitation
opts.B: Check the summary's statements against the original tender document
opts.C: Run the same prompt again and circulate whichever output is longer
opts.D: Ask the AI to rate its own confidence and accept it if the rating is high

exp: An AI summary is only a draft until it has been verified against the source, because a confident tone is a property of the model's writing style and not evidence that the content is accurate. A model's self-reported confidence is generated the same way as the rest of its text and is therefore not an independent check.

q: In India, financial cyber fraud and other cyber crimes can be reported on the national cyber crime helpline number:
exp: 1930 is the national cyber crime helpline, and complaints can also be filed online at cybercrime.gov.in; reporting a financial fraud quickly improves the chance of the money being held. 155260 was the earlier helpline number for financial cyber fraud and has since been replaced by 1930, while 1091 is the women's helpline and 112 is the general emergency number.

q: An employee receives an email that appears to be from the Treasury Department, warning that his account will be suspended within two hours unless he clicks a link and re-enters his login details; the sender's address ends in a domain unconnected with the government. The strongest indication that this is a phishing attempt is:

opts.A: The email arrived as plain text rather than in HTML format
opts.B: It manufactures urgency and asks for credentials from a non-official sender domain
opts.C: The email addresses the recipient by his designation instead of his name
opts.D: The email contains a hyperlink to an external website

exp: The classic phishing signature is artificial time pressure combined with a request for credentials from an address that does not belong to the genuine organisation's domain; a real department never asks for a password by email. A hyperlink on its own is not suspicious, since legitimate official mail routinely contains links.
